Capt Safdar's remarks about women suffering from illness draw criticism, including from CM Maryam. LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s spouse, retired Capt Muhammad Safdar, has come under fire for disparaging remarks about women advocating for bodily autonomy. Speaking at a Khatm-i-Nabuwwat rally in Chiniot earlier this week, Safdar took aim at the slogan “ mera jism, meri marzi ” (my body, my choice). He questioned why women who assert control over their bodies turn to religious scholars for prayers when diagnosed with serious illnesses such as cancer. “They say, ‘My body, my choice.’ But when they fall ill or develop cancer, they turn to religious scholars, seeking prayers and blessed water for a cure. They should understand that if they claim ownership over their bodies, they should also be able to cure them. In reality, the human body is under God’s control,” he said. On Friday, Maryam responded to a post on X regarding the speech, which stated: “Maryam Nawaz’s husband, Captain Safdar, also lost his mother-in-law to cancer, yet here he is mocking women who are battling cancer.” The chief minister’s mother, Kulsoom Nawaz, passed away in 2018 after a months-long battle with cancer. “Heartbreaking,” the chief minister said, posting an emoji of a broken heart. “The silent battles a woman, a wife, fights behind closed doors … The strength she must find even when she feels like breaking. Some battles are fought in silence and some wounds are invisible,” she said. Apart from CM Maryam, users on social media also took issue with Safdar’s remarks. “My [mother] has been a cancer patient, and God knows how we managed to get through those difficult times. Her survival was nothing short of a miracle. Listening to Capt Safdar’s remarks on this matter is utterly shameful and disgraceful!” said TV anchor Ajmal Jami on X. He also thanked CM Maryam for her “thoughtful and compassionate words for all those brave women”. Another user, Maheen Ghani, said: “So a woman who says ‘ mera jism, meri marzi ’, which is essentially about autonomy and consent, loses the right to ask for prayers when she gets cancer? Is that seriously the argument? “To take a woman’s illness, her fear and her faith and turn them into an opportunity to humiliate her. What an ugly, twisted understanding of both women’s rights and religion.” On the other hand, some, like journalist Benazir Shah, lauded CM Maryam for speaking out. “It takes real courage to take a public stand like this. More power to you, Maryam Nawaz Sharif,” she said. Lawyers’ bodies condemn remarks about Asma Jahangir Meanwhile, two premier lawyers’ bodies on Saturday strongly condemned Safdar for his remarks about Asma Jahangir – a renowned senior lawyer and human rights activist who passed away in 2018. During the rally, Safdar had called the late lawyer “cursed”. Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) Vice Chairman Pir Muhammad Masood Chishti, as well as the 28th executive committee of the outgoing Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), regretted the remarks and urged public representatives to exercise restraint and uphold dignity in their statements. Chishti called upon the relevant authorities to take immediate notice and initiate appropriate legal action. “The use of disparaging language and references to her religious identity to malign her is highly regrettable and deserves strong condemnation,” the PBC vice chairman regretted, adding that making such remarks against a deceased woman, who was no longer alive to defend herself or respond, was particularly “deplorable and reflects a lack of decency and respect”. The PBC vice chairman observed that differences of opinion must never become a pretext for personal attacks, hate speech, character assassination or religious intolerance. “The invaluable services and contributions of the late Asma Jahangir to the legal fraternity, human rights and the rule of law deserve respect and recognition,” he emphasised. Likewise, the 28th executive committee of the SCBA strongly and unanimously took exception to the recent remarks by Safdar. “These remarks are highly condemnable and have deeply wounded the sentiments of the entire legal community,” the SCBA said, adding that Jahangir was a devout Muslim who dedicated her life to justice, humanity, and the rights of all people, without discrimination. “Her services to humanity and human rights transcended religious boundaries and to make such hateful remarks about her was not only deeply disrespectful but also an insult to all those who continue to honour her legacy. She stood for the rights of every individual without discrimination.” The SCBA also strongly condemned derogatory remarks by Safdar against women and an illness that was “being valiantly fought back by hundreds of thousands of women across the world”. “At a time when women are breaking barriers, such remarks are disgraceful and entirely unacceptable,” the SCBA said. “What makes this conduct even more shameful is that his own spouse holds the highest office of Punjab chief minister, and he himself is the father of a daughter; he should have been ashamed of making such insensitive and degrading remarks directed against the women,” it said. These statements may also attract penal consequences, the SCBA reminded and called upon the concerned authorities to take immediate and strict notice and proceed in accordance with the law. “Such divisive, offensive, and intolerant attitudes must be firmly challenged and nipped in the bud. “Let it be clear to all and sundry, we will not remain silent when the dignity of our legal fraternity, the legacy of a human rights champion, and the respect owed to women are attacked,” the SCBA statement said. Nasir Iqbal from Islamabad also contributed to this report.

Sindh CM Murad blames city planners for 'ruining' Karachi. Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah on Saturday blamed urban planners for “ruining” Karachi, adding that he saw the metropolis vastly expand and deteriorate firsthand while growing up in it. In July 2025, a steering committee tasked with developing the Greater Karachi Regional Plan 2047 was informed that the new master plan of the country’s commercial capital would be ready within two years. Addressing an event of the Sindh Master Plan Authority (SMPA) in Karachi, CM Murad said: “Making a master plan from scratch is easy. But considering Karachi’s deteriorated condition, it is a challenge for consultants, master planners and urban developers to fix those [conditions], and also for the executive bodies to implement the plan.” CM Murad noted that SMPA , established under the Karachi Development Authority (KDA) in 1968, was formed to develop urban master plans for Sindh’s cities with recommendations from stakeholders. The chief minister said 14 master plans had been completed, but plans for Karachi and Hyderabad were under development. However, a post by the CM House quoted him as saying that master plans for 17 cities were complete, with work on 14 in final stages. Recalling that he grew up in Karachi and saw the metropolis’ expansion firsthand, Murad said, “I do not think any other city in the world has expanded as quickly as Karachi has, nor has any city in the world been ruined by planners as quickly as Karachi has.” The chief minister, whose PPP has ruled Sindh for about 15 years, stressed that Karachi needed to be improved. He contended that from the 1960s to the 1980s, it was a “very well-planned” city which attracted foreign visitors. Recalling an incident during the severe rains of 2020, Murad lamented that while travelling along a new dual-carriageway road from Yousuf Goth , he saw that people had set up shops along the side roads, the stormwater drains on either side of the main road and even on the median. “The planners did a very good job, but … a lot of roads have been declared commercial in the city and, to give people a livelihood, they are allowed to set up shops on stormwater drains for very cheap rent,” he said. “I request the help of all stakeholders in [solving] this issue. Unless the entire city comes together to make it better, then we will not be successful.” CM Murad also regretted that on several occasions, development work faced challenges due to delays from utility service providers, including the water board. He also pointed out the lack of mapping of utility infrastructure: “There is no mapping anywhere.” Noting Karachi’s population of 25 million and how urban development work inconveniences Karachiites, the chief minister said that funds have been arranged to rework 143 roads, but the work had not started because of procurement issues, which he said, “take a lifetime, but that’s how things are”. However, he stressed the importance of forums under SMPA to discuss urban planning and implementation. “These types of forums, seminars and discussions will help us bring some improvement and right now, in every city … the mayors and divisional headquarters are all trying to emulate the development which has started in Karachi.”

Fakhar Zaman and Arafat Minhas lead Pakistan to tri-series glory. Pakistan chased down 326 to beat Sri Lanka by three wickets in the final of the tri-nation series on Saturday at a packed Gaddafi Stadium, sealing the title with nine balls to spare in what was the joint-highest successful chase in an ODI final. Shaheen Shah Afridi, the captain, finished it in style — a six slapped over midwicket off Dilshan Madushanka in the 49th over — after Hasan Nawaz had levelled the scores with a dab to backward point. Pakistan finished on 327 for seven in 48.3 overs. For Fakhar Zaman, this was an innings that answered the questions swirling around his place in the side. He had spent much of the first innings off the field after copping a blow while fielding, and came out to open with his team 22 for two inside four overs and the chase already wobbling. His early stay was scratchy. He was dropped on three by Madushanka at deep third, and again on 69 by Mahesh Theekshana, who put down a return catch and later tipped a six over the rope. But from the wreckage of Pakistan’s top order he built an innings of substance, adding 149 with Saad Baig, who made 74 off 75 in his maiden half-century. Fakhar reached his 20th ODI fifty in the 22nd over, then his 12th ODI century in the 30th, pulling Asitha Fernando in front of square off 84 balls. He was finally bowled by Madushanka for 127 off 99 — 11 fours and six sixes — charging and missing a slog in the 34th over, walking off to a standing ovation from a full house. It was, by common consent, a vintage Fakhar innings on the biggest occasion. If Fakhar held the chase together, Arafat Minhas won it. The all-rounder walked in at 230 for five in the 37th over with Pakistan needing 96 from 78 balls, and played the innings of his young career — 61 off 31 balls, with three fours and four sixes. His check-drive six over long-on off Madushanka in the 46th over was the shot of the night, and his two sixes and a four off Asitha in the 47th brought the target within sight. He fell in the 48th over, caught-and-bowled by Asitha, and the Gaddafi Stadium rose as one. Sri Lanka’s innings Pakistan had won the toss and elected to field, and the decision looked sound early as Sri Lanka’s openers Kamindu Mendis and Avishka Fernando scored briskly without risk, taking the visitors past 50 without loss inside ten overs. Pakistan had brought in Faheem Ashraf for Shadab Khan, ruled out on medical grounds after being struck by a bouncer in the fifth ODI, while Sri Lanka replaced the pace of Eshan Malinga with the spin of Mahesh Theekshana. The contrasting selections suggested both sides had read the conditions differently, and Pakistan’s pace attack struggled for early impact. It was Salman Ali Agha who provided the breakthroughs, claiming both wickets to fall before the final ten overs. Avishka missed a sweep and was leg-before in the 18th over, and four overs later Kusal Mendis stepped out and drove the ball back at Salman, who leapt to take a superb return catch. Beyond those two dismissals the innings belonged to Kamindu, who took charge through the middle overs and brought up his century in the 34th over, cutting Faheem over the wicket-keeper’s head. Pavan Rathnayake gave him valuable support, the pair adding 146 for the third wicket, with Rathnayake making 77 off 65 balls. Kamindu’s 131 off 128 balls, with 12 fours and two sixes, anchored the innings. At 238 for two after 40 overs, Sri Lanka looked set for a total beyond 350. But Pakistan’s death bowling pulled it back. Shaheen trapped Kamindu leg-before in the 42nd over and dismissed Dasun Shanaka soon after for a brisk 17 off nine. Haris Rauf had Rathnayake caught by Babar Azam at wide long-on, and he and Naseem Shah removed Dunith Wellalage and Sahan Arachchige in quick succession. Naseem’s wayward penultimate over let Sri Lanka past 320, but they lost six for 70 in the last ten overs to finish on 325 for eight. Pakistan’s innings Pakistan’s reply began badly. Maaz Sadaqat charged Madushanka in the second over and edged to slip for five, and in the fourth Babar Azam, under scrutiny for his form, drove at a floated delivery and was caught by a solitary fourth slip — a trap set by Kusal Mendis and executed to perfection. Babar departed for a five-ball duck, and Lahore went quiet. From there on , Saad joined forces with Fakhar and steadied Pakistan’s innings. Saad brought up his maiden half-century in the 19th over, and Fakhar reached his 20th ODI fifty in the 22nd. The pair added 149, and Fakhar rode his luck — dropped on three by Madushanka, and again on 69 by Theekshana. Saad fell for 74 off 75, chipping a full delivery back to Theekshana in the 27th over. Fakhar, growing fluent, reached his century in the 30th over. Salman Agha made 17 before Wellalage bowled him with one that skidded under his slog sweep, and Fakhar’s innings ended in the 34th over, bowled by Madushanka for 127. That left Pakistan 220 for four, needing 106 from 96 balls, and when Salman fell at 230 for five the game was alive again. Hasan Nawaz and Arafat Minhas steadied, then accelerated. Arafat’s 61 off 31 turned the chase, and he and Hasan added 50 off 49 balls. Asitha removed Arafat, caught-and-bowled, and Faheem Ashraf first ball in the same over to briefly raise Sri Lankan hopes, but Hasan and Shaheen held their nerve, and the captain’s six sealed it. The win is Pakistan’s first ODI tri-series title since the Kitply Cup in Dhaka, when they beat India in the final, and it comes days after they were bowled out for 110 by this same Sri Lankan side in the league stage — a collapse that had raised fresh questions about the batting. Those questions were answered, at least for one night, by Fakhar, whose place in the side had itself been under discussion, and by Arafat, whose striking drew comparisons with a genuine match-winner. The dew that Pakistan had hoped for arrived late, but by then the hosts had found their own momentum. Sri Lanka, who had chased 430 against England in the league stage, will rue the missed chances — two lives for Fakhar, a dropped catch and a boundary conceded at deep cover — and a death-overs collapse with the bat that left them just short of a total that might have been enough.

1 dead, over 13 injured during stampede at TikToker's mehndi ceremony in Sialkot. NAROWAL: A stampede at a mehndi (henna) event and prize-distribution ceremony held by a TikToker in Sialkot left one person dead and more than 13 others injured last night, police and rescue officials said on Saturday. The mehndi ceremony and prize-distribution event for Muhammad Ansar Jatt, a popular TikToker from Sialkot district known as “Mr Pattlo”, was scheduled for Saturday night at Faraz Cricket Ground on Daska Road, according to a statement by Rescue 1122. In a statement, the Sialkot police said that as event organisers opened the stadium gates to allow attendees in, a stampede ensued and many fell to the ground. Citing initial information, it said 14 people were injured. Among those, 30-year-old Muhammad Aqeel passed away while being transported to the hospital due to his critical condition, the Rescue 1122 statement said. Sialkot police said they and Rescue 1122 personnel conducted a joint rescue operation and transported the injured to Allama Iqbal Memorial Teaching Hospital. Most of the individuals were discharged after receiving first aid, while others remained under medical care, the statement added. According to Rescue 1122, the injured persons comprised men aged between 22 and 51 years, and hailed from various districts, including Narowal, Gujranwala, Sheikhupura, Khanewal, Okara, Sialkot, Gujrat and Bahawalpur. However, Sialkot residents Muhammad Asif and Aamir Ali stated that more than 40 people were injured in the stampede, explaining that before the rescue teams arrived, attendees had taken several injured to nearby private hospitals and clinics for first aid on their own. Sialkot District Emergency Officer Engineer Naveed Iqbal said the rescue service had not been informed in advance about the large gathering planned at the cricket ground. He added that four ambulances and one motorcycle ambulance participated in the rescue operation. Following the incident, Sialkot District Police Officer (DPO) Dost Muhammad had also reached the site, accompanied by a large police contingent and the Elite Force. Acting on the DPO’s instructions, the police took charge of security arrangements, brought the crowd under control, and ensured that rescue operations could proceed without interruption, the police statement said. Speaking to Dawn , DPO Muhammad criticised the event organisers for opening the stadium gates ahead of schedule. The retired captain noted that granting permission for such an event fell under the purview of the district administration. The DPO emphasised that the protection of the lives and property of citizens remains the police’s top priority. All aspects of the incident will be examined and appropriate legal action will be taken, he asserted. Dawn has reached out to Sialkot Deputy Commissioner Awais Mushtaq for comment.

Pakistan slams Afghan Taliban for 'shifting blame', 'persistent refusal' to address terrorism issues. The information ministry on Saturday rebuked the Afghan Taliban’s stance on the ongoing conflict between the two countries, assailing its “persistent refusal to address terrorism” emanating from Afghanistan’s soil. The statement came in response to remarks made by Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid, who blamed Islamabad’s “wrong policies” for preventing a resolution to the conflict and insisted Kabul was not the cause of counterterrorism issues. “Pakistan does not want to resolve the conflict with Afghanistan through talks,” Mujahid told Hurriyat Radio , claiming that Islamabad “lacks the necessary readiness for a peaceful resolution of differences”. In its statement, the information ministry said the Afghan spokesman’s remarks expose the “regime’s deeply misguided approach and unwillingness to confront the root cause of deteriorating relations with Pakistan”. “The Taliban leadership continues to blame Islamabad’s policies while conveniently ignoring the single most important issue poisoning bilateral relations: its persistent failure to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil,” it added. The ministry reiterated Pakistan’s “unequivocal” position: terrorism is a red line and the security of its citizens is non-negotiable.* “The Afghan Taliban regime must understand that Pakistan will not tolerate terrorist sanctuaries across its borders that impact its security nor allow its people to remain targets of terrorism emanating from Afghanistan,” it stated. Islamabad reiterated that the “Taliban regime’s persistent refusal to address terrorism remains the principal obstacle to normal relations”. “Shifting blame, making hollow assurances and questioning Pakistan’s policies will neither resolve the crisis nor absolve Kabul of its responsibilities. The Afghan Taliban leadership must understand that Pakistan’s security will not be held hostage to Afghan Taliban’s inaction, evasions or misplaced priorities. ” The information ministry affirmed that Pakistan reserved the right to “take all necessary measures, in accordance with international law, to eliminate threats to its national security, wherever they originate”. It urged Kabul to recognise that the responsibility for addressing these threats “rests squarely with the Afghan Taliban regime”. “Pakistan’s resolve to protect its people must never be mistaken for weakness,” it declared. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. Multiple rounds of talks between the two sides last year, facilitated by Qatar and Turkiye , failed to bring about any workable solution, with the Pakistani government saying the Taliban officials gave no assurances on the key issues. Efforts this year made with China’s involvement also resulted in no breakthrough. September witnessed another bout of conflict between the two neighbours, with Pakistan carrying out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. This was followed by drone incursions from across the border, which Islamabad said were shot down, and two further rounds of retaliatory airstrikes. Those skirmishes continued in October, with Pakistani security forces responding to unprovoked fire from the Afghan side along the border in Kurram and Lower South Waziristan’s Angoor Adda , according to security sources. On Tuesday, Afghan security forces opened unprovoked fire on border posts and residential areas in the Angoor Adda border area, which claimed the life of one local and injured a family of five.

Germans join Europe's wave of 'Gen Z' protests; police fire water cannon on demonstrators. German police fired a water cannon to disperse firework-hurling protesters on Saturday and were also pelted with other projectiles, as tensions rose at the end of massive youth-led protests. In Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and dozens of other cities, demonstrators turned out for the protests organised by the group ‘ GenZ regelt! ’ (GenZ has got this), the latest by disillusioned youth in Europe. Thousands of police were deployed across the country and, after mostly peaceful demonstrations, tensions rose in the evening in some places. In the western city of Cologne, where one of the biggest demonstrations took place, police fired a water cannon to disperse a crowd after saying protesters had targeted officers with fireworks. “We will not tolerate violence against emergency workers,” said a police statement. Protesters light dlares after a demonstration organised by “GenZ regelt!” (Gen Z has got this!) in Frankfurt am Mian on October 31, 2026. — AFP Earlier, a march through the city was halted after demonstrators started setting off fireworks. A march was also temporarily halted in Frankfurt after protesters set off fireworks. In Berlin, protesters hurled bottles and eggs while protesters set barricades ablaze in Hamburg, and police were using pepper spray on demonstrators in some places, Germany’s daily Bild reported. Demonstrators had earlier taken to the streets waving signs that read “Time for resistance” and “Merz must go”, in reference to conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz. They have been inspired by similar movements across Europe, including in France and Italy . Europe-wide protests “We’re taking to the streets for a life that everyone can afford,” said Veronika Dinter, a spokeswoman for the “ GenZ regelt! ” movement. “Hardly anyone still believes in a better future if everything just continues as it is.” The movement’s complaints range from the high cost of living to poorly maintained schools, government spending cuts and, more broadly, what it sees as politicians making decisions with apparently little regard for the younger generation. They are also unhappy with sharply increased military spending and a new voluntary service model aimed at boosting troop numbers, fearing it is a step towards bringing back conscription. Riot Police bloct the street in front of protesters after a demonstration organised by “GenZ regelt!” (Gen Z has got this!) in Frankfurt am Mian on October 31, 2026. — AFP Several thousand demonstrators turned out in Cologne while the figure was around 5,000 in Berlin and 8,000 in Frankfurt, according to police. There were also sizeable gatherings in other parts of the country, although the numbers were below the 170,000 nationwide that organisers had hoped for. Authorities have been worried the protests, coinciding with Halloween, could be marred by the same kind of violence seen elsewhere in Europe. Protests were also taking place in France for a third straight weekend. Nationwide demonstrations there on Oct 17 degenerated into some of the country’s worst rioting in years. Berlin is in contact with officials in France and Italy amid fears that radicals from overseas could seek to join the German protests. A policeman stands next to police cars on the sidelines of a demonstration organised by “GenZ regelt!” (Gen Z has got this!) in Berlin on October 31, 2026. — But prior to the protests, authorities said that they had not seen evidence of concrete plans for violence. The “ GenZ regelt! ” movement explicitly rejects violence. It stresses that “extremist groups, anti-constitutional symbols, racism and hate speech have no place with us — no matter from which side”. Christian Volk, an expert in protest movements, said there was the potential to see a major movement emerge in Germany. But Volk, from Berlin’s Humboldt University, told AFP there were key differences with France, which has a “completely different tradition when it comes to confrontational forms of protest”.

‘Very little, if anything, done for KP’: PM Shehbaz rails against PTI’s governance in province. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday criticised PTI’s governance in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, questioning whether the funds available to the now dysfunctional provincial government had been used transparently for the welfare and betterment of the people of the province. His remarks came during a meeting of the PML-N’s parliamentary party from KP, held in Islamabad. The Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Oct 11, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move had drawn criticism from the opposition, as well as Fazl , who had made efforts to reduce tensions between the federal and the KP governments. Taking aim at the PTI, Prime Minister Shehbaz said: “They have been in power in KP for 13 years. Over these 13 years, they have raised countless slogans, delivered fiery speeches, held long marches and sit-ins, and made numerous promises.” Recalling PTI’s promises to build hundreds of dams, generate hundreds of megawatts of solar power, and establish hospitals, universities and schools across the province, the prime minister questioned whether any of these pledges had been fulfilled during the party’s 13 years in power. “How many universities have been established there? How many new hospitals have been built? How much has the healthcare system improved? What facilities have actually been provided to the people? And how much corruption has taken place in the process?” he asked. The prime minister also questioned whether public funds had been utilised transparently for the welfare and betterment of the people of KP. “From Peshawar to Kohistan and Hazara, and across the entire southern region of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the majority of people would tell you that the PTI government has done very little, if anything, to address their basic needs,” he said. The premier maintained that by 2017-18, terrorist activities in the province had been brought to an end to “a considerable extent”. “Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was among the provinces that made the greatest sacrifices in the fight against terrorism,” he said. The prime minister highlighted the heavy toll terrorism had taken on the country, saying around 80,000 people had lost their lives and Pakistan’s economy had suffered losses estimated at Rs15,000 billion. He also praised former prime minister and PML-N supremo Nawaz Sharif for his policies to combat terrorism following the 2014 Army Public School tragedy , in which more than 140 students and teachers were killed. Turning to the PTI, the prime minister said the party had spent the past two and a half years engaged in long marches and protests. “In 2014, Chinese President Xi Jinping was scheduled to visit Pakistan. We made repeated efforts to persuade the party to call off its sit-in so that President Xi’s visit could proceed as planned, but it refused. As a result, the visit was postponed ,” he said, recalling the 2014 D-Chowk protest. He also criticised the PTI for allowing “brutal terrorists” from Afghanistan to settle in Swat. “These were among the most painful and heartrending incidents that allowed terrorism to regain momentum,” he said. The premier further said that thousands of civilians and security personnel had been martyred during the past two and a half years, adding that the PTI had been offered an opportunity to join hands with the federal government to combat terrorism , as it had done in the past. He also said that hundreds of billions had been allocated to the KP government under a special National Finance Commission (NFC) arrangement to combat terrorism. “How many Safe City projects have been initiated in KP? How much money has been spent on strengthening the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD)?” he asked. The prime minister elaborated that even if the PTI-led KP government had spent Rs80 billion on strengthening the police and other law enforcement agencies, they would have been better equipped to tackle security challenges. “But unfortunately, that did not happen,” he added. He said the federal government had managed to put the national economy back on its feet, but acknowledged that the recovery process would be a long journey. The prime minister recalled that the government had formed a committee comprising members of the PPP and PML-N to hold talks with the PTI. “Both sides held negotiations for 48 hours. I was told that the draft had been finalised and would be signed within minutes, following approval from then-chief minister Sohail Afridi. However, the approval never came, and we are still waiting,” he said. PM Shehbaz said the federal government was compelled to impose an emergency and governor’s rule, as it had no other option. He emphasised that the Centre’s decision had been “timely”, warning that the consequences would have been severe had it been delayed. The prime minister urged PML-N lawmakers from KP to prioritise the basic needs of the people in their constituencies, while putting long-term projects on hold for the time being. “Focus on short-term welfare projects so that you can help turn people’s fortunes around within the next six months to a year,” he stressed. PTI hits back at PM’s criticism Meanwhile, the PTI hit back at the premier’s criticism, challenging the federal government to account for its own record instead of blaming the party for KP’s security and governance problems. PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram said the prime minister had no moral authority to lecture the party on democracy and governance, alleging that the present political setup had come into power through electoral manipulation and political arrangements. Waqas accused the federal government of shifting responsibility for the province’s worsening security situation onto the PTI provincial government. He alleged that the federal government had failed to provide the province with necessary resources and equipment for counterterrorism operations. He also accused the Centre of focusing on political opposition rather than addressing security and governance issues, alleging that PTI leaders and workers had faced raids, arrests and intimidation. He also challenged the premier to present a comprehensive account of his government’s four-year performance. Less than a week after emergency and governor’s rule were imposed in the province, a joint sitting of parliament approved the federal government’s move amid a strong protest from the opposition. The events of Oct 11 followed weeks of political tensions between the Centre and the PTI — as well as negotiations to bridge their differences — after the latter announced a long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. Federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups and asserted that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks . The PTI said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre denied . It also called for reviewing the counterterrorism policy, while the latter criticised the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objected to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. Nuclear science boosts Pakistan’s ability to track groundwater. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has strengthened its ability to track groundwater resources using nuclear science, enabling scientists to identify recharge sources, determine groundwater age and trace contamination pathways, according to an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) report released on Saturday. The Regional Cooperative Agree­ment (RCA) for Research, Deve­lopment and Training Related to Nuclear Science and Technology for Asia and the Pacific, Hydrology and Groundwater programme has significantly enhanced Pakistan’s capacity for continuous groundwater monitoring through the application of isotope-based techniques. This advancement has considerably strengthened the connection between scientific research and water governance, allowing for more precise and systematic observation of groundwater dynamics across diverse hydrogeological settings, the IAEA report said. Studies undertaken through RCA-supported projects have generated reliable estimates of groundwater recharge rates, aquifer interconnections and pollution pathways in key regions such as the Indus Plain, the Quetta Valley and the Cholistan Desert. IAEA report says RCA-backed isotope techniques help country trace water sources, age, pollution pathways These findings have deepened the scientific understanding of Pakistan’s groundwater systems while providing essential inputs for developing long-term strategies for water reso­urce management, the agency noted. Prior to joining the programme, groundwater monitoring was not a primary focus of national hydrological investigations. Several studies were conducted using conventional methods, such as hydro-chemical analyses and physical measurements, but these approaches provided only basic information on water table depth, water quality and aquifer dynamics. Through its participation in the programme, Pakistan has significantly strengthened its laboratory capacity for isotope hydrology. The Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science and Technology (Pinstech) now hosts one of the region’s most advanced isotope analysis facilities, complemented by 12 laboratories nationwide. Currently, Pinstech and the Pakistan Council of Research in Water Resources work in close collaboration to incorporate isotopic data into national groundwater management models. “This integration supports the early detection of over-extraction, salinity intrusion and other forms of aquifer stress, thereby contributing to more sustainable groundwater utilisation,” the report said. The focus on data-driven management has fostered a stronger culture of evidence-based decision-making within national and provincial water institutions. Policymakers are increasingly rel­ying on isotope hydrology data to inf­orm regulatory frameworks, resource allocation and long-term planning, reflecting a significant shift from reactive to preventive and science-informed groundwater management. Pakistan’s participation has delivered substantial economic, social and environmental benefits. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

‘Medicine pricing needs serious attention’. KARACHI: More than 86,000 medicines produced by pharmaceutical companies have been registered under the Track and Trace System, allowing consumers to scan products by mobile phone to check their authenticity and find out their prices, Federal Health Minister Mustafa Kamal said. He said that pharmaceutical companies could also register their medicines and products online. A process that previously took years is now being completed within just 21 days. Addressing the members of the Korangi Association of Trade and Industry (KATI) on Saturday, he said the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) has been made fully transparent and digitalised. Eight months had passed since DRAP’s certification procedures were shifted to a digital system, during which more than 5,000 cases had been processed, he said. Mustafa Kamal said the issue of medicine pricing requires serious attention. The pharmaceutical industries seek an increase in medicine prices, but the matter is under consideration by the federal cabinet. The issue has two dimensions as an increase in medicine prices will create additional financial difficulties for ordinary citizens, while keeping prices unchanged could lead to shortages of medicines for serious illnesses. Consequently, patients were sometimes forced to purchase the same medicines from the black market at three times their actual price. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

SMOKERS’ CORNER: THE MYTH OF PTI’S POPULARITY. For years, political analysts across the board, from pro-Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) commentators to supposedly neutral and anti-PTI observers, insisted that PTI was the most popular political party in the country. This narrative was even widely echoed by Western media outlets. Lately, however, that conviction has eroded. Commentators first began backtracking by limiting their claims about PTI’s dominance to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), but even that has started to falter. What many mistook for widespread support may simply have been what political scientists refer to as “manufactured popularity.” Manufactured popularity is not a reflection of unmediated public sentiment. Instead, it is a carefully crafted construct accumulated through symbolic engineering, media management, state or institutional sponsorship, and the strategic exploitation of public disillusionment. At its core, manufactured popularity depends on presenting a leader as a spotless saviour, who is capable of dismantling a ‘corrupt’ old order. This form of popularity is built on exaggerated promises and carefully curated media narratives. But the moment an engineered project makes the transition from opposition to executive power, tensions between rhetoric and governance begin to dissolve the illusion. Throughout history, political regimes and movements have demonstrated how manufactured popularity can decay when confronted with cold realities. In the 1950s, former president Juan Perón’s initial popularity in Argentina was sustained by heavy state subsidies and nationalistic appeals. Yet, as economic historian Carlos Díaz-Alejandro documented in his analyses of Argentine economic history, the regime’s inability to sustain fiscal extravagance amidst soaring inflation and foreign exchange depletion eventually caused Perón’s populist economic model to unravel, hastening widespread unrest and military intervention. While PTI’s online dominance is often taken as proof of overwhelming public support, digital visibility, electoral success and the ability to mobilise people on the streets are three very different measures of political strength In post-communist Eastern Europe, the rise and fall of political movements that relied on media-driven anti-corruption narratives, such as Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha’s movement in Bulgaria during the early 2000s, illustrate that popularity constructed primarily on outsider status and high moral claims quickly evaporates when administrative ineptitude and economic compromises take hold in daily governance. PTI, formed by Imran Khan in 1996, is an intriguing example. It remained a minor player on the margins of Pakistani politics till its transformation into a dominant force in 2011. The transformation was not merely an ‘awakening’ but also a carefully constructed political phenomenon. PTI’s popularity was methodically cultivated, mainly by the military establishment. Indeed, the party effectively mobilised a real sense of grievance among urban middle-class voters who were exhausted by the perceived ‘corruption’ of traditional parties such as the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP). But this was amplified by institutional engineering through a hybrid scheme. According to the Pakistani political scholar Muhammad Waseem, in this scheme, intelligence agencies steered the media narrative, weakened political opponents, and directed influential political “electables” towards PTI. Illustration by Abro The architecture of PTI’s popularity was heavily built on a modern communication strategy. According to the media researcher Ifrah Nadeem, PTI pioneered the use of “computational propaganda.” It unleashed tightly targeted social media campaigns, and emotional messaging. By leveraging digital spaces, the party bypassed mainstream journalistic scrutiny, portraying Khan as an incorruptible reformer who alone could usher in a ‘Naya [New] Pakistan.’ According to economists such as Atif Mian and academic assessments by the International Crisis Group, governing a state such as Pakistan that is under severe balance-of-payments distress required unpopular policy adjustments. But this contradicted PTI’s idealised campaign claims. So, when Khan was placed in power in 2018, the election of an ‘honest leader’ was framed by the party as a good enough condition for economic revival and institutional purification. But Khan blundered his way across almost all vital areas of governance. This resulted in the gradual pullback of the military establishment’s patronage of his regime. Therefore, the manufactured framework sustaining the government collapsed, culminating in Khan’s removal via a constitutional vote of no-confidence in 2022. The erosion of manufactured popularity reveals a recurring dynamic in politics. According to the American political scientist Samuel P. Huntington, while media manipulation, emotional appeals and institutional patronage can create an impression of overwhelming public approval, they cannot transform into tangible administrative competence and economic stability. While failing leaders who were elevated through manufactured popularity often switch to narratives of victimisation or conspiracy to retain a dedicated core, the initial perception of popularity begins to alter when tested by on-ground political realities. But here’s the interesting bit: even after Khan’s fall, the narrative of his ‘popularity’ did not recede as such. At least not in the media. Political commentators and international monitoring groups viewed the support for PTI-backed candidates in the 2024 general elections as proof of this. However, one can posit that this was largely achieved through PTI’s formal and informal social media apparatus transitioning the party’s narrative from that of producing an incorruptible saviour to one of moral victimisation. In the aftermath of Khan’s arrest in 2023, PTI’s media apparatus cleverly converted the general public anger over rising inflation and political instability (which Khan’s regime left behind), into an unquestioning loyalty to the imprisoned Khan. This was further reinforced by digital algorithms that amplified symbolic/performative acts of resistance, creating an impression of impressive public mobilisation. However, the eventual reality check occurred when the limits of this online and sentiment-based popularity were tested on the ground. The definitive moment arrived when the current coalition government-imposed emergency measures and governor’s rule in KP recently, sidelining PTI’s provincial government there. Contrary to expectations of an uprising, the public response was muted. The failure of the party to mobilise street demonstrations underscored a disconnect between online sentiment and real-life capacity. This led political analysts to re-evaluate the nature of the party’s popular base. They began recognising that much of what had been interpreted as deep political commitment was, in fact, passive sympathy, digital noise, and an anti-establishment protest vote rather than an organised, resilient political movement. The illusion of overwhelming popularity unravels when passive sympathisers who express support on social media or through voting, decline to transform into active political actors on the streets. They are in the majority, and many are even stationed abroad. The loss of PTI’s last institutional foothold in KP demonstrates that, while manufactured popularity and grievance-based narratives can maintain an electoral pull, they remain inherently fragile when confronted with state power, and the reality of growing public apathy. The electoral pull too is now likely to recede, especially with the likelihood of Khan remaining behind bars in the foreseeable future. Published in Dawn, EOS, November 1st, 2026

LPG price twice the official rate in open market. • Ogra notifies about Rs15 per kg increase in gas price • Association warns of strike from Nov 16 over new LPG policy ISLAMABAD: As the government again notified an increase in the price of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for November, its price in the open market is twice as high as the official rate amid a shortage of LPG due to the US-Iran war. In a notification on Saturday, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) notified Rs294,075 per tonne for November compared to Rs279,341 in the previous month. Following the increase, the official retail rate of an 11.8 kg domestic cylinder of LPG is Rs3,470, up by Rs173. The official LPG rate is Rs294 per kilogramme. The oil and gas regulator said that the LPG producer price was linked with Saudi Aramco-CP and the US dollar exchange rate. It added that compared to the previous month, Saudi Aramco-CP had increased by 6.47 per cent, while the average dollar exchange rate had slightly decreased by 0.12pc, resulting in an increase in the LPG consumer price by Rs14.73 per kg. In the open market, LPG is selling for up to Rs630 per kg, while the company-operated franchises are charging up to Rs400 per kg, with many warning that the crisis would compound due to the gas shortage. LPG Distributors Association of Pakistan Chairman Irfan Khokhar said that the situation was serious because of the Iran border closure . He said at least 70 per cent of LPG was imported from Iran, while only 30pc was locally produced. “The government has to make serious efforts to control market manipulations,” Mr Khokhar added. On the other hand, LPG marketing companies thre­atened to shut down their businesses from Nov 16 if the private sector was sidelined in the upcoming LPG policy. Pakistan LPG Marketers Association Cha­irman Ali Haider warned that they will observe a strike from Nov 16 if the government implemented the policy. He said the government should not reverse the deregulation of LPG, adding that the gas was in short supply due to the Iran border closure. “Out of around 1.3 million tonnes, only around 225,000 is imported from the Gulf, and that too has been mainly imported by the private sector,” he said, adding that the ProGas terminal at Port Qasim was under the control of the Sui Southern Gas Company which “imported LPG around seven months back”. The association also wrote a letter to Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, stating the draft policy sent to the prime minister had no input from the private sector. The association called for the complete deregulation of the LPG sector. It said the 2016 LPG policy imposed Rs4,669 per tonne petroleum development levy on locally produced LPG. This was imposed to provide subsidies to the state-owned entities such as the PSO, Parco, and SSGC to import LPG during winters and in any emergency, like the current scenario. “Despite billions of rupees collected in terms of PDL through this formula, the state-owned entities have failed to import LPG during these days,” Mr Haider alleged. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

US to deport 150 Afghan immigrants back to Kabul. WASHINGTON: President Don­­ald Trump’s administration plans to deport more than 150 Afghan immigrants back to Afghanistan via Pakistan, US media reported, a move advocacy groups say could endanger their lives. Trump last year issued travel bans for a number of countries, including Afghanistan, as part of a broad immigration crackdown, and sought to end deportation protections for Afghans, some of whom were granted special immigrant visas following the August 2021 takeover by the Taliban. More than 150 Afghan immigrants are expected to be deported in the latest push, The New York Times reported on Friday, citing three unnamed US officials, and the first flight could leave as soon as Monday. Among those expected to be deported are relatives of Afghans who assisted the US military in the country prior to the fall of Kabul, according to AfghanEvac, a group seeking to help former Afghan allies. While the US cannot arrange deportations directly to Afgha­n­istan, the officials told the Times that Pakistan will oversee their expulsion to Afghanistan. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

Islamabad High Court bars FIR mention in character certificates after acquittal. ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) has ruled that police cannot mention an FIR in the character certificate of a citizen who has been acquitted in the case, declaring any such certificate unlawful and invalid. Justice Ayyaz Shaukat, while deciding a public interest petition, directed the Inspector General of Police, Islamabad, to establish a formal mechanism to ensure that references to criminal cases ending in acquittal are not included in character certificates issued to citizens. The court observed that citizens should not be compelled to approach courts to exercise rights already guaranteed under the law. It held that following an acquittal, there was no legal justification for portraying an individual as an accused or criminal through a police-issued character certificate. Rules such mention violates constitutional rights, including dignity and freedom of movement Allowing the petition, the court ordered the removal of a reference to an FIR registered at Shalimar Police Station from the petitioner’s character certificate. The judgement clarified that although police could maintain internal records of criminal cases for official purposes, such information could not be disclosed in character certificates issued to citizens, particularly when these were required for travelling abroad. It further observed that there was no legal basis for mentioning an FIR in a character certificate after the proceedings had culminated in a final acquittal. Any certificate containing such a reference would be legally invalid. Justice Ayyaz Shaukat also rejected the police’s description of the petitioner as having been “discharged” during the investigation, observing that such a characterisation undermined the legal effect and status of the acquittal. The court held that including an FIR in a character certificate despite an individual’s acquittal violated Articles 4, 9, 14 and 15 of the Constitution, which protect citizens’ rights, liberty, dignity and freedom of movement. It emphasised that a person acquitted through due process of law could not continue to face adverse consequences through a character certificate suggesting involvement in criminal proceedings. The court directed the Islamabad police chief to introduce a proper procedure to ensure that acquitted citizens did not have to initiate fresh litigation merely to obtain character certificates reflecting their actual legal status.
