Uncertain local governments. THE battle between the Election Commission of Pakistan and the provincial and federal governments has been an almost permanent feature of Pakistan’s electoral scene since 2010, when the responsibility for holding local government elections was entrusted to the Commission under the 18th Amendment. Currently, the ECP is fighting a four-way battle — with the provincial governments of Punjab and KP, the federal government, and the cantonment boards — for LG elections in the two provinces, Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT), and the cantonment boards. The LGs in Sindh and Balochistan (except in the largest district of Quetta, where the entire term passed without election) have yet to complete their terms. The ICT LG election is the most disappointing case. The last LG election in ICT was held in November 2015. Its five-year term ended on Feb 14, 2021. Under the Elections Act, 2017, the new election was to take place within 120 days after the previous LGs’ term ended, making June 15, 2021, the due date for the next election. For more than five years, the ECP and the federal government have been haggling over legal points and the possible date of the next election. Since 2021, the ECP has issued the election schedule four times and carried out fresh delimitation five times. Each time it has had to eat humble pie by withdrawing the schedule as the federal government changed the goalposts and amended the LG election law. The latest in the series was the ICT Local Government (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, promulgated on Jan 10, 2026, which drastically changed the capital’s LG system. However, the ordinance lapsed in September 2026. While parliament is going through the motions of converting the lapsed ordinance into an act of parliament, the ECP maintains that the old ICTLGA, 2015, stands resurrected after the ordinance lapsed and, therefore, issued a polling schedule on Oct 25, fixing Dec 20 as polling day. Looking back at the federal government’s track record, the new act is likely to pass in the next few days, after which the ECP would have no choice but to withdraw the schedule and begin preparations anew. The case of KP is not very different; the terms of the LGs expired on June 19, 2026, after which new elections should have taken place by Oct 20, but the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local Government (Amendment) Act, 2026,was passedand became effective on July 16 this year. It changed the size of the village and neighbourhood councils. The ECP strongly objected to the amendment, termed it a delaying tactic, and asked the provincial government to review the law. In the meantime, the ECP is proceeding with preparations to hold the LG polls, except in 12 districts where the law and order situation doesn’t permit polls. The ECP has yet to issue an election schedule. Still, it remains to be seen whether the National Assembly, which has the legislative powers of the KP Assembly after the proclamation of emergency, will amend the LG law or whether the elections will be postponed yet again on some pretext or the other. The ECP is battling both the federal and provincial governments that are reluctant to hold LG polls. All formalities for holding the LG election in Punjab have been completed by the ECP and the Punjab government under the Punjab Local Government Act, 2025. If finally held, this will be the first LG election in roughly 11 years. The election was supposed to be held in May 2022, but a series of new laws and amendments kept postponing it. Although the Punjab government ministerial committee and the ECP agreed to hold the election in three phases between Dec 15 and Jan 15, the Punjab government changed its mind and asked the ECP to defer the election until April 2027 because of dense fog and school exams in December. The ECP immediately rejected the new dates and asked its secretariat to prepare an election schedule based on the earlier agreed dates. The election schedule has not yet been issued; one should wait to see which side blinks first. The election to 43 cantonment boards in the country was due on Aug 8 as the four-year term of the previously elected boards expired on April 11, 2026. The cantonment boards’ election has an additional prerequisite: the ECP should receive the federal government’s request before holding the election. Reportedly, no such request has been received, and the ECP, given the legal requirement to hold elections within 120 days of the expiry of the term, is trying to reach out to the federal government. Regardless of the outcome of these efforts, the election to the cantonment boards is also overdue. These four stories lead to a single conclusion: both the federal and provincial governments are reluctant to hold LG elections on one pretext or another. The key flaw in the system is that while the ECP is responsible for holding LG elections, the governments and their legislatures alone write the LG laws. There is no bar on legislatures amending LG laws. As demonstrated repeatedly, the law can be amended after the announcement of the election schedule and even a few days before polling day, undoing all the preparation made by the ECP such as delimiting LG boundaries. The solution is for parliament to amend the Elections Act, 2017, and bar any amendment to the LG laws after the expiry of the LG term, so the ECP can prepare unimpeded and hold timely elections. As if these difficulties were not enough to make the future of LGs uncertain, another layer of unpredictability has been added by the possibility of carving out new provinces and, in the case of ICT, by the announcement that Islamabad may soon have provincial status. This may give the government yet another pretext to slow-walk LG elections. The writer is the president of Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.president@pildat.org X: @ABMPildat Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

India’s water blackmail. SINCE April 2025, when India unilaterally suspended the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), most scholarship has treated it as a political decision by the BJP-led NDA government. While it is true that the BJP has been developing a narrative that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi was ‘rectifying’ the ‘mistakes’ of the Nehruvian era, the decisions and developments during the past 18 months suggest that New Delhi is developing a long-term strategy to strangle Pakistan economically. India’s primary target in this strategic campaign is the Chenab river, which it is systematically converting into a long-term instrument of leverage to dictate Pakistan’s foreign policy, weaken its stance on Kashmir, and dominate bilateral relations. In the 18 months since it decided to keep the IWT in abeyance, India has aggressively leveraged this treaty vacuum to build a massive network of storage, regulation, and diversion infrastructure on the Chenab. New and accelerated hydroelectric power projects, primarily concentrated in the Chenab basin, have ballooned from a baseline capacity of 3,263 MW to 7,620.5 MW, supported by a massive financial outlay of approximately Indian rupees 414.04 billion. No single dam or diversion canal can permanently dry up a river. However, a highly synchronised, connected network of mega structures, coupled with diversion canals, can fundamentally determine who controls the timing and volume of river flow. India is trying to apply a two-pronged strategy, ie, increase storage capacity and enhance the ability to divert the Chenab’s water. India’s strategic roadmap involves five megaprojects alongside extensive local diversions. This includes Sawalkot (1,856 MW), Kirthai I & II (1,320 MW), Pakal Dul (1,000 MW), Ratle (850 MW), and Bursar Storage (800 MW). India’s infrastructure push began in May 2025, with the announcement of the tender for the Uri-II project (240 MW), followed quickly in June 2025 by the tender announcement for the Dulhasti-II project (260 MW). Activity accelerated in July 2025 with two major announcements — first, a tender for the removal of deposited sediments from the Salal Dam Reservoir, and second, the Sawalkot project (1,856 MW) tender under international competitive bidding. In March 2026, civil contracts were officially awarded for both the Uri-I stage II and Dulhasti stage-II projects, alongside the official tender announcement for the highly controversial Chenab-Beas Link Tunnel Project (Link-3). These aforementioned projects command a combined potential diversion and storage capacity of roughly 7.287 MAF. For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic foundations. The Chenab-Beas Link Project is particularly consequential. With a reported budget of Indian rupees 23.52bn, it proposes to transfer water from the Chandra river, a major Chenab tributary, through an 8.7-kilometre tunnel into the Beas basin and onward through a 113km canal network to eastern Indian states. The proposed diversion of 1.9 MAF annually from the Chenab basin raises serious questions about compliance with Article III of the IWT. The threat of manipulation, or the Chenab’s vulnerabilities, poses a direct risk to Pakistan’s economic survival, social stability, and national security. The Chenab directly irrigates agricultural lands across more than 11 districts of central Punjab, the country’s undisputed food basket. These districts form the densest core of the famous rice-wheat cropping zone. This 11-district area accounts for about 22 to 25 per cent of Pakistan’s national food grain output. If India controls water flows during October to December or May to July, it may affect seasonal yields in this zone. In such a scenario, it could cause a direct blow of $9bn to $11bn to Pakistan’s economy. The broader impact would ripple through the national economy in several ways. Pakistan would be forced to spend billions of scarce foreign exchange reserves to import basic food commodities. Instead of generating $3.3bn to $4bn from booming rice exports, the country would face a multibillion-dollar trade deficit just trying to secure alternative grain imports. Second, any sustained restriction on, or unpredictable disruption to, these water flows would threaten the livelihoods of millions of farming households, while endangering crops and compromising national food security. Therefore, Islamabad must view India’s decision to place the IWT in abeyance as another dimension of New Delhi’s long-standing and coordinated policy of economic strangulation of Pakistan. For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic foundations. New Delhi has been consistently trying to restrict Islamabad’s access to global capital and limit its trade capacity. A primary example is India’s aggressive lobbying within the Financial Action Task Force, where it has consistently tried to politicise technical compliance and block Pakistan’s removal from the grey list to discourage foreign direct investment and cripple its banking sector. Beyond regulatory warfare, India has systematically disrupted regional trade platforms, such as Saarc, effectively stalling economic integration across South Asia to keep Pakistan regionally isolated. Faced with this asymmetric threat, Islamabad’s response has been largely concentrated on the external front. Pakistan’s state apparatus has consistently pursued international legal and diplomatic channels. However, a dangerous policy gap exists on the domestic front. Ground-level preparedness is profoundly lacking. The agrarian communities, provincial irrigation departments, and economic sectors that will bear the immediate impact of India’s upstream infrastructure remain highly vulnerable. Pakistan lacks the modern water-storage infrastructure, optimised canal lining, crop-switching strategies, and real-time early warning systems needed to survive sudden changes in river flows. Hence, Islamabad should complement its legal and diplomatic efforts with urgent domestic reforms. Pakistan must declare a national water emergency, educate vulnerable communities in 11 districts of central Punjab that depend on the Chenab, expedite dam construction, and modernise irrigation. Without urgent preparedness, Islamabad will risk surrendering its agricultural security to Delhi’s water blackmail. The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

Consumer firms defy economic headwinds. KARACHI: Amid rising food inflation and weakening purchasing power from higher fuel costs driven by Middle East tensions since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on Feb 28, local and multinational consumer goods companies in Pakistan reported improved sales in the first nine months of 2026 and the first quarter of FY27. However, some companies remain cautious about their full-year 2026 outlook amid persistent inflationary pressures. Nestlé Pakistan Nestlé Pakistan’s net sales for the nine months ended Sept 30, amounted to Rs160bn, up 6.3pc from the corresponding period last year. Despite rising inflation, political instability and higher fuel and energy prices amid the US-Iran war, the company sustained its business momentum. It attributed its performance to increased investment in brands, product innovation and renovation (I&R), stronger marketplace execution, improved export channels and disciplined pricing, where necessary. Local and multinational companies post robust sales growth this year Net profit after tax rose 3.1pc to Rs14.526bn from Rs14.1bn a year earlier, despite higher tax expenses. In response to geopolitical uncertainty, the company accelerated localisation and secured essential inventories to reduce foreign exchange exposure, strengthen supply chain resilience and ensure uninterrupted operations. Citing geopolitical instability, volatile energy and input costs, and persistent inflation, Nestlé maintained a cautious outlook for 2026. FrieslandCampina Engro Pakistan FrieslandCampina Engro Pakistan’s revenue increased 10.1pc to Rs88.4bn in the first nine months of 2026 from Rs80.2bn in the corresponding period last year. The company attributed the growth to a favourable product mix, stronger market execution and selective investment in brands. Profit rose to Rs6.5bn from Rs2bn a year earlier. Regional conflicts, higher freight and energy prices put pressure on the company’s operations and input costs during the third quarter of 2026. In Pakistan, inflation and interest rates also constrained household purchasing power, affecting product affordability and demand, the company said. Unilever Pakistan Unilever Pakistan Foods’ sales rose to Rs37.6bn in the first nine months of 2026 from Rs30bn a year earlier, while profit after tax increased to Rs6.326bn from Rs4.6bn. Unilever said Pakistan’s economy remained resilient, supported by higher foreign exchange reserves, fiscal consolidation and a gradual recovery in economic activity. However, renewed inflation, higher global commodity and energy prices, and Middle East tensions continued to constrain consumer spending, the company added. Colgate-Palmolive Pakistan Colgate-Palmolive Pakistan’s sales rose 25.53pc to Rs52.7bn in July-September 2026, driven by higher prices and sales volumes. Profit after tax increased 8pc to Rs4.9bn compared with the corresponding period last year. The company said persistent inflation, tax collection constraints and high energy tariffs continued to pose challenges. Regional tensions also posed supply chain risks because of its reliance on Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries for essential raw materials. Fauji Foods Fauji Foods Limited (FFL) recorded its highest-ever nine-month revenue of Rs23.9bn in 2026, up 14.1pc from the corresponding period last year. However, profit after tax fell to Rs666m from Rs945m. Despite inflationary pressures on consumption, FFL reported growth across its product portfolio. National Foods Limited National Foods Limited’s sales rose to Rs11.1bn in July-September 2026 from Rs10bn a year earlier, while profit increased to Rs888m from Rs801m. According to Rabia Yousuf of Topline Securities, National Foods informed shareholders at its 55th annual general meeting, held recently, that it expected revenue growth of 15pc in FY27, with scope for further improvement if macroeconomic conditions improved. She said management highlighted a rise in freight rates from $500-$600 to $5,000 per container. Continuing tensions in the Middle East may also constrain export volume growth. Management plans to launch more than 25 products and remains optimistic about expanding its portfolio. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

In Spectrum: Gymkhana: colonial origins and politics of selective outrage. The British did not establish clubs in colonial India merely for cricket, golf and other recreations. They formed part of the social architecture of colonial rule, providing civil and military officials with spaces to cultivate networks, consolidate solidarity and preserve racial distinctions. The exclusion of Indians from establishments reserved for Europeans reflected the belief that political domination conferred social superiority. This history deserves unequivocal condemnation. Yet condemning an institution’s colonial origins does not automatically invalidate its subsequent existence. Institutions, like societies, can evolve, and their ability to transcend the circumstances of their creation is an important measure of historical adaptation. Lahore Gymkhana emerged from this world of colonial exclusivity and acquired its present name on March 23, 1906. Its history, however, cannot be frozen at the moment of its inception. Partition in 1947 dismantled the political and social order that had sustained colonial institutions, yet Lahore Gymkhana survived and gradually became part of the civilian life of ‘independent’ Pakistan. An institution originally designed for a privileged foreign establishment adapted to a different national and social environment, drawing members from professional, business and salaried circles. While it remains selective and cannot be described as wholly egalitarian, its contemporary identity is no longer synonymous with the racial exclusivity of its founders. It should be borne in mind that salaried individuals are among those whose incomes are taxed at source, and the revenue generated through taxation helps meet government expenditures without relying solely on loans from international institutions. Those crying foul over Gymkhana are privileged individuals who, in many cases, do not bear their fair share of the tax burden. Anyhow reverting to the transformation deserves recognition, particularly in a country where many inherited institutions changed their personnel after independence without fundamentally altering their hierarchical structures. Lahore Gymkhana’s evolution illustrates the possibility of preserving institutional continuity while accommodating a changed society. Its achievement lies not in perpetuating colonial privilege but in acquiring a different social meaning. Its history should, therefore, be assessed in the context of what it has become, rather than reduced to the circumstances of its birth. Its internal electoral system is another important dimension of this evolution. The election of office-bearers by members provides a mechanism of representation and accountability, distinguishing member-based civilian governance from systems dependent entirely on external authority or official appointment. The transparency of these elections must be judged by the electoral rules, eligibility criteria, fairness of the process and publication of results. Elections alone do not guarantee flawless governance, but neither should an established electoral system be dismissed without examining its actual functioning. Internal democracy does not make a club universally accessible, just as selective membership does not automatically make it unaccountable. These are distinct questions and should be treated as such. This combination of historical continuity, social adaptation and member-based governance makes Lahore Gymkhana a distinctive institution in Pakistan’s civic landscape. Its survival is not remarkable merely because it has endured; its significance lies in its ability to acquire a place in a society radically different from the one that produced it. This transformation should neither be romanticised nor dismissed. It deserves recognition alongside an honest examination of the institution’s remaining privileges and obligations. It is against this background that the current criticism of the club must be judged. Its centrally located land is undeniably valuable, and questions concerning its lease, construction approvals, taxation and financial obligations are legitimate. No institution should be exempt from the law, and public property must be administered transparently. But accountability is only as credible as the evidence supporting it. The manner in which a member of the provincial assembly reportedly questioned the club’s chairman raises concerns if inaccurate examples or questionable comparisons are presented as established facts. Parliamentary oversight is a serious responsibility, not political theatre. An elected representative’s authority should be reflected in the accuracy of his information and the fairness of his questions, not merely in the audacity of his confrontation. The selectivity of this indignation is equally troubling. If public land must be administered equitably, the principle must apply to all institutions, irrespective of their influence or proximity to the state. What comparable scrutiny is directed at garrison clubs, golf courses and other establishments associated with powerful constituencies? What standards govern their leases, concessions and use of public resources? These questions do not absolve Lahore Gymkhana of accountability; they expose the inconsistency of targeting a civilian institution while comparable arrangements elsewhere may escape equivalent examination. If low rents, unauthorised structures or tax irregularities are objectionable, the same standards must apply across the board. Otherwise, equality before the law becomes a slogan invoked against the accessible while the powerful remain undisturbed. The value of the club’s land inevitably raises another concern: whether scrutiny is directed towards a genuine public benefit or could create an opportunity to transfer a valuable asset from one privileged constituency to another. The land’s commercial potential makes vigilance necessary, although it does not, by itself, prove that any particular critic is motivated by land-grabbing interests. If the lease is legally defective or financially indefensible, it should be reviewed through lawful procedures. But reclaiming valuable property is not automatically an act of public service. The authorities must explain what would replace the existing arrangement, who would benefit and whether the city would gain genuinely accessible recreational space or merely another commercially valuable development. Reform must serve the public, not simply change the beneficiaries of privilege. Lahore Gymkhana should, therefore, be judged on two distinct but related grounds: the legality of its present arrangements and the significance of its institutional transformation. Its colonial origins cannot be condoned, but neither should they become a permanent indictment of an institution whose social context and governance have changed. Its lease must withstand legal and financial scrutiny; its elections should be assessed for transparency; and its evolution after Partition should be recognised without exaggerating its egalitarian character. Acknowledging institutional progress does not mean granting immunity from accountability. The real test of accountability is consistency, just as the test of institutional progress is the capacity to change. Pakistan must do more than condemn the exclusions of the Raj: it must subject contemporary privilege to equal scrutiny, regardless of who enjoys it. To single out a civilian club while leaving comparable or greater concentrations of privilege insufficiently examined is not a triumph of democratic accountability but a contradiction of its central principle. An independent society demonstrates its maturity by judging institutions impartially, recognising genuine adaptation, demanding transparency in the use of public resources and refusing to let political theatre replace evidence. Lahore Gymkhana’s colonial past should remind us of the injustice of exclusion; its subsequent evolution should remind us that institutions can change. The ultimate standard must be the public interest, not selective indignation or the lure of valuable urban land. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

World Bank okays $150m plan to boost property tax collection in Karachi. ISLAMABAD: The World Bank has approved a $150 million programme to help the Sindh government improve urban property tax collection and strengthen municipal service delivery in 25 towns of Karachi. The Sindh Property Revenues Enhancement Programme (Sindh PREP) approved by the World Bank board of executive directors, will benefit Karachi’s 25 local councils. Its primary beneficiaries are the 3.58 million people living in these councils, where service delivery investments will be financed, the World Bank resident mission in Islamabad announced on Saturday. The programme will support the Sindh government in improving urban immovable property tax (UIPT) collection and strengthening municipal service delivery capacity in selected local councils of Sindh. “Cities that can raise their own revenues can plan and invest for the long term,” said Bolormaa Amgaabazar, World Bank Country Director for Pakistan. “Today, Sindh’s local councils depend on provincial transfers for more than 95 per cent of their revenues. By helping Karachi collect the property taxes from its residents and businesses, and by reinvesting most of that revenue in local services, this programme will give Sindh’s cities the means to finance the infrastructure they need.” About 70 percent of collected UIPT revenues will be reinvested directly into municipal infrastructure and services in participating local councils. “Karachi has significant untapped potential to generate revenues from its property base and use those resources to fund the infrastructure its residents and businesses need. This programme will help Sindh strengthen fiscal sustainability enabling cities to plan, invest, and deliver services from their own resources effectively,” said Davison Muchadenyika, senior urban development specialist at the World Bank. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

Binance to resume withdrawals after covering bulk of stolen $6.3bn. Binance, the worlds biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said it would resume withdrawals on Sunday after covering 95 per cent of the $6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform in the world’s largest digital heist, which the FBI has tied to North Korea. The exchange, founded in China, said the first phase of withdrawals would start between 0600 and 0900 GMT and cover 15 crypto assets including bitcoin, ether, XRP, dogecoin and others. Binance said on Sunday it had covered $6bn of stolen cryptocurrencies by using company money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5pc of stolen tokens consist of assets that are less liquid and may take longer to source in the required amounts, according to the exchange. FBI ties attack to North Korea unit The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. The FBI said on Saturday the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment. Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected “further laundering” of the assets through the use of related technology. Analysts had blamed North Korea and said the Binance theft could be the largest financial heist of all time. The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. US President Donald Trump, however, said on Saturday that the US was still not certain if North Korea was involved. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea but if it is, we’ll talk to North Korea about it,” Trump told reporters on Saturday in comments posted by a White House handle on X. Binance vows to bear financial costs Binance has been working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3bn located as of Friday, it said. The exchange has repeatedly said it would bear the financial impact of the funds stolen in the hack. It has set aside around $6.34bn of company funds internally to cover the losses. The money spent buying replacement tokens came from Binance’s $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users( Safu), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and its corporate treasury, it said on X. Co-CEO Yi He said on Saturday that 50pc of its Safu funds would be used, while the company committed to replenishing the fund to about $1 bn. Richard Teng, the other co-CEO, has said that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate. Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe after the hack. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.

North Korea tests cluster-bomb warheads: KCNA. North Korea test-fired cluster-bomb warheads, its state media reported on Sunday, the latest in a slew of weapons drills aimed at training its military units on using them. The test, conducted on Saturday, came after the nuclear-armed North recently trialled a range of weaponry including attack drones, a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile. It also came against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded. The North has denied responsibility and vowed to further fortify its border areas and resume its loudspeaker campaign. Saturday’s test was conducted to “assess adaptation to combat and power of a cluster-bomb warhead to be tipped on tactical ballistic missiles”, the official Korean Central News Agency reported on Sunday. Officials said it confirmed the weapon “is capable of turning into ashes a target area of 12 to 13 hectares with its highest-density power”. “Within this year we will enable units to select and use all those types according to operational aims and specific features of targets,” said the general director of the North’s Missile Administration. Photos released by KCNA showed a projectile firing from a mobile launcher, with an orange exhaust plume. Another image showed multiple cluster-bomb impacts on an island target. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un was not present on Saturday, although he had overseen a test-launch of cluster-bomb warheads mounted on a ballistic missile in April, accompanied by his daughter Ju Ae .

US hears Pakistan’s concerns over terrorism from Afghanistan, would play ‘productive role’ if there is one: Rubio. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday said that Washington has “heard” Pakistan’s concerns about terrorism emanating from Afghanistan and if “there’s a productive role for us to play, we would play it”. Rubio’s statement came in response to a question about tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan at a press talks in Atlanta. “Pakistan is concerned about terrorist attacks that are being sponsored from the territory of Afghanistan. They feel as if the Taliban have not done enough to constrain those attacks, and they have taken action against it. “We obviously have heard those concerns on their part. We obviously don’t want them to be targeted for terrorism. So if there’s a productive role for us to play, we would play it,” Rubio said. Mentioning that the US did not “necessarily [have] the closest relationship” with the Afghan Taliban, Rubio added: “We’ve heard the concerns that Pakistan has raised and we’ve seen some of those attacks that they point to. We’re against terrorism no matter where it emanates from and who it targets.” Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), that it says are used for attacks in Pakistan. For their part, the Afghan Taliban have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while rejecting Islamabad’s allegations that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan. On Saturday, Pakistan’s information ministry rebuked the Afghan Taliban’s stance on the ongoing conflict between the two countries, assailing its “persistent refusal to address terrorism” emanating from Afghanistan’s soil. The statement came in response to remarks made by Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid, who blamed Islamabad’s “wrong policies” for preventing a resolution to the conflict and insisted Kabul was not the cause of counterterrorism issues. In its response, the information ministry said the Afghan spokesman’s remarks expose the “regime’s deeply misguided approach and unwillingness to confront the root cause of deteriorating relations with Pakistan”. “The Taliban leadership continues to blame Islamabad’s policies while conveniently ignoring the single most important issue poisoning bilateral relations: its persistent failure to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil,” it added. Islamabad reiterated that the “Taliban regime’s persistent refusal to address terrorism remains the principal obstacle to normal relations”. Multiple rounds of talks between the two sides last year, facilitated by Qatar and Turkiye , failed to bring about any workable solution, with the Pakistani government saying the Taliban officials gave no assurances on the key issues. Efforts this year made with China’s involvement also resulted in no breakthrough. Russia, the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government, has also recently renewed its offer to facilitate a settlement if both sides request its involvement. Moscow’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, had last month made this suggestion after the latest round of the Moscow Format consultations on Oct 5 ended without a joint communiqué because of differences between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban delegations over references to terrorist networks operating from Afghanistan. When asked about it during a weekly media briefing , Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan had said talks with Afghanistan could not be unconditional. He also rejected suggestions that Islamabad was unwilling to engage with its neighbour, saying it would welcome sincere efforts by friendly countries to help resolve the dispute. He further stated: “At present, I am not aware of any separate, formal Russian mediation initiative being under discussion.” Meanwhile, intermittent skirmishes at the border continue. September witnessed yet another bout of conflict between the two neighbours, with Pakistan carrying out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Those skirmishes continued in October with Pakistani security forces responding to unprovoked fire from the Afghan side along the border in Kurram and Lower South Waziristan’s Angoor Adda , according to security sources.

Broken record: constitution, commander, curfew.. The issues of Dawn from Sept 1-7, 1947 chronicled the adoption of the Pakistan (Provisional Constitution) Order as the country’s working constitution, while the nation’s first commander-in-chief issued a stern call for order to control communal violence. Moreover, the city of Karachi — which has been no stranger to violence over the decades — saw its first curfew as the capital of Pakistan. Constitutional underpinnings Constitutional tinkering by powerful, often unelected forces has been a sad constant throughout Pakistan’s history. But as the pages of Dawn in the weeks after independence showed, the country’s founders wanted the country to be run as per the rule of law, not anyone’s personal whims. The lede story in the Sept 3, 1947, edition noted that “the Pakistan (Provisional Constitution) Order, an adaptation of the Government of India Act, 1935” would serve as the dominion’s temporary constitution. Of course Pakistan would not have its first proper constitution until 1956, largely owing to the political tumult of the early years. The Pakistan (Provisional Constitution) Order sought to do away with the vestiges of empire, and give a fresh direction to the country. The news story noted that the law “does away with expressions like “in his discretion” and “exercising his individual judgment”, found in the India Act.” “Another important feature is absence of any reference to the King anywhere. All appointments including those of the provincial Governors and High Court Judges, will be made by the Governor-General.” Moreover, the oath of office would be sworn to the “Pakistan Constitution and not to the Crown.” From these reports, it is clear that the original plan envisaged a farewell to British kings and queens, and constitutional supremacy. Little did the founders of Pakistan know that in the decades to come, many uncrowned local ‘kings’ would trample the Constitution, and attempt to dictate terms to the hapless populace of this country. The general’s call Two weeks after independence, the fires of communal violence continued to burn, despite repeated appeals by none other than the Quaid for calm. The situation was such that the Pakistan’s army’s first commander-in-chief — Gen Sir Frank Masservy, a British officer — issued a plea for peace in the Sept 1 issue. In a special order to all ranks of the army, the C-in-C noted that “our main duty … in conjunction with the civil authorities and the police is the difficult and unpleasant one of maintaining law and order and of stopping bloodshed and murder, looting and arson. …” The general told his men that there would be zero tolerance for law breakers and other undesirables that were stirring up trouble. “The first type of goondas are goondas , dakus and badmashes . These are enemies of the State and must be hunted out and captured or shot. … “The second type are ignorant citizens and countrymen who get carried away by feelings of revenge … and vent their wrath on the opposite community with the utmost savagery. These two are also enemies of the State tough they may not realise it. …” These were certainly stern words from the general. But perhaps desperate times called for desperate measures. Petrol rationing Pakistanis, as well as consumers around the world, are paying high prices for gasoline and other fuel products derived from hydrocarbons due to the situation created by the US/Israeli war on Iran. There is also the fear of shortages should things get ugly again in the Gulf; in other countries, there have been riots related to fuel shortages, though Pakistan has thankfully been spared such violence till now. In Sept 1947, however, the state had to resort to rationing of gasoline as communal disturbances in India had disrupted supplies of coal, putting extra pressure on the available fuel stocks. As a news report highlighted in the Sept 2 issue, “the Government of Pakistan has decided to reduce the present ratio of motor spirit from two gallons per unit to one gallon per unit, in Western Pakistan. This step is taken in order to conserve all the available fuel supply. …” The decision was made “owing to the disturbances in East Punjab” which had caused interruption in the regular supply of coal to Pakistan from India. Karachi under curfew Younger readers, particularly those born in the mid-1990s and thereafter, would not have any memory of a curfew clamped on Karachi. But older readers will recall with dread the days and nights the metropolis used to be placed under curfew during the 1980s and early 1990s due to the rampant political and ethnic violence of those bad old days. In effect it was an order from the state to shelter in place; unless you had a curfew pass, the law-enforcement agencies — often including the military — would not let you move about freely to quell spasms of violence. But the first curfew in the history of Karachi after Independence was clamped on Sept 4, 1947, to help contain communal violence. A report in the Sept 4 issued said that “Mr N.A. Faruqi, District Magistrate, Karachi, today enforced curfew on the major part of Karachi from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. The curfew will last for three days. It has been imposed under Section 144 CrPC.” The next day, in the Sept 5 issue, the headline of the lede story on p1 declared, with some relief, that ‘Karachi’s first curfew night passes off peacefully’. The story went on to say that “No incident was reported in the city till Friday afternoon. Shops and other business quarters worked normally and except for the exodus of a large number of Sikhs and [Hindu] Marwaris by sea to ports in Bombay, there was nothing abnormal … in the city.” The exodus, we were told, “was not because they were afraid of the Muslims in Pakistan, but of the “insanity” of their brethren in the Indian Union.” Palestine partition Overseas, the UN’s partition plan for Mandatory Palestine was igniting emotions across the Arab world. As the banner headline on p1 in the Sept 2 issue declared: ‘Arabs to resist Palestine plan by force of arms’. As Israel has expanded its illegal occupation of Palestine over the decades, the Arabs are still resisting. A news report filed from London declared that “Arab leaders in Jerusalem, Cairo, London and New York last night rejected the recommendations of the United Nations Special Committee for the partition of Palestine as “blatantly unfair” and declared that the Arabs would resist the plan even by the force of arms.” Meanwhile, armed Zionist gangs such as Irgun called for a “prolonged war against the British” who administered Palestine at the time. With the advantage of hindsight, one has the opportunity to study the historical cycles in a nation’s life. Thanks to this newspaper’s unique, extensive archive of back issues, one can examine the major political, economic and social trends that have shaped Pakistan and the world over the last seven decades and counting. Cliched as it may sound, history repeats itself, and we — as a state and as a polity — largely refuse to learn from it. Through this platform, we will look back at the ‘big’ stories that made it to the front pages of Dawn, as well as significant developments tucked away in the inside pages, from the birth of Pakistan onwards, and try to put them in perspective. We will study the critical issues of the week, starting from Aug 14, 1947 and examine the major themes and issues that made it to the paper.

Thousands protest in India's capital against voter roll revision. Thousands joined a protest led by opposition politicians in India’s capital on Sunday, renewing demands for the country’s election chief to resign over an overhaul of voter lists they say unfairly benefits the ruling party. The nationwide revision of electoral rolls has sparked political disputes and street protests in the world’s largest democracy over the last month. The Election Commission says the initiative is necessary to ensure accurate voter lists, but the opposition claims it is being manipulated to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the Election Commission and the BJP deny the accusations. On Sunday, protesters led by opposition Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi chanted “vote thief, leave your seat” and beat drums while marching from central parts of New Delhi to Ramlila Maidan, a large outdoor venue. “I have been a voter since I was 18 and now I find myself struck off the list,” protester Nandita, 46, told AFP , giving only one name. “It’s important to be here because of the way things are going. The cost of living is going up… The only option is to take to the streets peacefully.” The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online youth-led protest movement, has also thrown its weight behind the campaign against the voter-roll revision. The overhaul of India’s voter rolls has resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings. Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims . Members of Hindu-nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls. Election authorities say the revision was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries, and that eligible voters remain entitled to apply for inclusion on the roll. Human Rights Watch has said the removal of voters was “arbitrary and deeply flawed”. “The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalised people their right to vote and other government services,” it said in a statement this week. The Cockroach movement has been heavily involved in the pushback to the voter-roll revision and several of its leaders were temporarily detained by police during protests last month. The CJP has gained millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May. Earlier protests organised by the CJP in July over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi’s administration.

Till I am here, people of KP will have the first right to its resources: Kundi. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi asserted that the people of the province had the first right to its resources. “No one should think that foreigners will come and loot this province. Till I am here, the people of the province will have the first right to its resources,” he said while addressing a ceremony in Peshawar. Kundi added that a third party from outside KP, whether a foreigner or from Pakistan, may enter into a joint venture with the people of the province if willing. The governor, who has assumed the administrative control of KP following the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in the province, assured that his priority was the protection of the people of KP, then of the province itself and then Pakistan. His assertions follow allegations by Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman that the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in KP was linked to the government’s motive to take control of its resources. He had also questioned the government’s position on mineral resources during a National Assembly session earlier this week, when he had criticised the Centre over emergency and governor’s rule in KP. Meanwhile, claims have been circulating on social media that KP’s minerals would be given or sold to the US. This followed a statement made by Chargé d’Affaires Natalie Baker during an interview with The Centrum Media on Sept 30, expressing US interest in Pakistan’s mineral resources. Kundi, without making any specific mention, said in his address that several reports may be circulating in the media and on social media, but his priority remained the protection of the people of KP. He said this after outlining the diversity of KP’s resources: “Compared to other provinces, KP has the most natural resources and, as they say: Jahan wasail hotay hen wahan par masail bhi hotay hen (wherever there are resources, there will always be issues). KP is the largest oil and second-largest gas producer in Pakistan, and [..] we produce electricity. We have tourism, mineral resources, and tobacco.” Kundi also spoke of the Rs160 billion pledged by the federal government for development projects in KP. He said 70 per cent of the funds will be allocated to the 12 districts under the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) and 30pc to other districts. Kundi assured, “My brothers and sisters in the merged districts will not be deprived of their rightful share.” On alleged corruption charges against non-functional KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, the governor said if the charges were proven, due legal process would be adopted. On Friday, adviser to the KP governor on information and public relations Samar Haroon Bilour said that available evidence regarding financial corruption by Afridi was being compiled. Afridi remains in preventative custody and has not been seen since the imposition of governor’s rule in the province. The Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on October 11, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. Less than a week after emergency and governor’s rule were imposed in the province, a joint sitting of parliament approved the federal government’s move amid a strong protest from the opposition. The events of Oct 11 followed weeks of political tensions between the Centre and the PTI — as well as negotiations to bridge their differences — after the latter announced a long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. Federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups and asserted that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there.

Cyber safety. WHILE the state’s proposal to create a Cybersecurity and Social Media Awareness Council envisages needed interventions to protect children from online harm, the same body’s focus on ‘fake news’ — as described by the government — is cause for concern. Speaking at a recent seminar in Islamabad, the federal information minister said there is a need to raise awareness about the “dangers of fake news”, while also emphasising the need for digital education in schools and colleges. In particular, he said children should be protected from cyberattacks. At the same event, the IT minister observed that it was important for both parents and children to know who the latter were interacting with online. There can be little argument with the fact that cyberspace can be a dangerous place for children. According to a Unicef report , one in 16 children in Pakistan aged 12-17 experienced “at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse” in a single year. This comes to around 1.5m children. Moreover, the National Commission on the Rights of the Child points out that youngsters are vulnerable to “cyberbullying, online grooming, sharing of sexual abuse materials” and other types of harm. There have been disturbing recent reports of even parents and guardians involved in the online abuse of children. It is, therefore, essential to protect youngsters from online predators through digital literacy, while bringing those involved in these abominable crimes to justice. Pakistan’s children face enough challenges; the state must do all it can to protect them from online harm. But combining steps against cyberbullying and online abuse of children with the state’s campaign against ‘fake news’ needs to be reconsidered. The state of freedom of expression in Pakistan is already quite poor, so any further attempts to clamp down on free speech must be resisted. Instead, the proposed council should focus on protecting children from dangers in the cyber realm, as well as keeping citizens overall safe from online threats. Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

Pakistan becomes chair of G-24 bloc of developing nations, reaffirms pledge to fairer global financial system. Pakistan assumed the chairmanship of the Group of 24 (G-24) on Sunday, with Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb expressing the country’s resolve to strengthen the collective voice of developing economies and “advancing a more responsive, fair and development-oriented international financial system”. The intergovernmental group is a coalition of developing countries established in 1971 to coordinate their positions on international monetary and financial issues, according to its website. Aurangzeb described its chairmanship as a “profound responsibility”, a handout issued by the Ministry of Finance stated, adding that he also called for “renewed international cooperation, stronger multilateral institutions and reinforced global commitments to address climate shocks, development financing gaps and global economic fragmentation”. “The future of developing economies is not peripheral to the future of the global economy. It is central to it,” the statement quoted the finance minister as saying. He further highlighted the “immense potential of emerging and developing nations as drivers of investment, innovation, entrepreneurship and global growth”. Aurangzeb outlined three strategic priorities for Pakistan under the G-24 chairmanship: placing development at the centre of global economic policymaking, strengthening multilateral frameworks, and advancing a development-oriented international financial architecture. For the first priority, the finance minister stressed the importance of macroeconomic stability, saying it must underpin investment, productivity, employment, and shared prosperity. He added that such an approach would enable “developing and low-income economies to move beyond crisis management towards sustainable growth”. Secondly, he added that under its chairmanship, Pakistan would advocate for “more equitable and fair governance, meaningful participation in decision-making and greater responsiveness of the Bretton Woods institutions to the evolving needs and realities of their members”. Thirdly, the finance minister said Pakistan would prioritise affordable and timely development financing, sustainable debt solutions, stronger global financial safety nets, climate resilience and greater mobilisation of public and private capital. “Our task is to ensure that the immense potential of developing economies is not constrained by an international financial architecture that has yet to fully adapt to a changing world,” Aurangzeb was quoted as saying. The finance minister emphasised aligning financial stability with long-term development objectives, drawing on Pakistan’s experience with economic stabilisation, reform and resilience, the statement said. He added that this would ensure that reforming economies have the necessary financing and policy space to pursue sustainable growth. Aurangzeb further stated that Pakistan’s tenure as the chair would be guided by “G-24’s longstanding principles of consultation, consensus and collective advocacy, working closely with members across Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, alongside the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank and other international partners, to translate shared priorities into practical outcomes.” The finance czar acknowledged outgoing chair Nigeria’s leadership and pledged to build on the group’s progress. He further emphasised that the “effectiveness of collective leadership must be judged by tangible development outcomes”. “The true measure of our collective leadership will not simply be the strength of our voice, but the difference that voice makes,” the ministry quoted him as saying. According to the statement, Aurangzeb reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to advancing G-24’s mission “from collective voice to collective influence, and from collective influence to meaningful progress”. ‘Significant diplomatic milestone’ President Asif Ali Zardari hailed Pakistan’s assumption of the G24 chairmanship and congratulated Aurangzeb along with the relevant team. In a statement on X, he said the development was an “important” opportunity for the “effective” representation of developing countries in global economic affairs. “This opportunity will provide Pakistan with the chance to play a role in developmental financing, climate challenges, and promoting global financial cooperation,” the president asserted. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also welcomed the development, calling it a “significant diplomatic milestone” and expressing hope that the chairmanship would provide Pakistan “an opportunity to play an influential role in advocating for necessary reforms within the global financial system, securing equitable financial support to address climate change and promoting sustainable development opportunities for emerging economies”, a statement issued by his office said. He also lauded the finance minister and his team for their “tireless efforts, effective diplomacy, and professional competence”. The premier further commended the team for ensuring “impactful” participation at the recently held annual meetings of the World Bank and the IMF, which he said helped Pakistan secure a “prominent position in the economic leadership of developing nations”.

Pakistan’s past and future make a bid for the present. Whatever there is to be said about Fakhar Zaman has been said. And he has usually said it himself – first when he made his debut and steered Pakistan to their greatest triumph of the past decade, then countless times for Lahore Qalandars, then on that one rainy day in Bangalore, climbing a mountain no one had given him a shot at. Fakhar has had a long few years, with recurring injuries and patches of very lean form, but his penchant of showing up when it matters, in extremely emphatic fashion, hasn’t wavered with time. In a side that gets frequently noted for crumbling under pressure, faltering in the biggest moments, never being quite able to get over the line for true glory, Fakhar has churned out a reputation for himself that is the opposite. A ‘big match player’ is the sort of cliche that seems overwrought, but Fakhar has made it entirely his own. When it matters most, it is foolish to count him out. “The way my last 4 games had gone, a good performance was due,” he said during the post-match ceremony after scoring a match-winning century to lead Pakistan to triump in the One-day International tri-series final against Sri Lanka on Saturday. Fakhar Zaman celebrates his half century with Saad Baig alongside, during the tri-nation series final at the Gaddafi Stadium, Lahore, on Saturday, 31st October 2026.–AFP “Cricket is just like this, sometimes you are a good knick and sometimes you don’t score; even today I was struggling in the beginning.” “But I know that when it is my day, and the ball is coming onto my bat, I will score big.” And that he did – despite his lean returns in the first four matches Pakistan played in this tri-series, and despite the several scares he survived yesterday - wobbly shots, being dropped and given reprieves, Fakhar showed why giving him a life in a final has been, historically, a bad idea. Pakistan does not have a lot of time left with Fakhar. He is 36 years old, and will be 37 by the time next year’s World Cup in southern Africa is underway. It would probably be the most opportune moment for him to sign off on a memorable career, trying to give his team one shot at the ultimate glory in his favourite format. His century yesterday - 12th in ODIs, a record-breaking fourth in chases of more than 300 - is just one of those things Pakistan fans should learn to cherish when they get. But if yesterday showed anything, apart from reaffirming what Fakhar means to a Pakistan side, it was that Pakistan don’t have to be starved of time. In a match where Pakistan’s most trustworthy southpaw wielded his bat once again, it was one other that let him, and yet another that ensured it wouldn’t go to waste. Saad Baig had big shoes to fill coming into this ODI tri-nation series. With Mohammad Rizwan’s absence, Pakistan was not only missing a cog of the batting line-up that has been so crucial for so long, but also one of the finest pair of wicket-keeping gloves the country has sported. No one else has seemed good enough in comparison behind the stumps - either too undercooked, or too sloppy. Saad was Pakistan’s U-19 captain, and made his debut earlier in this tri-series. With a promising performance behind the stumps, and a string of starts with the bat that left one feeling unfulfilled but entirely assured of the pristine talent that shone through, the 19-year-old came out looking like he had a lot to prove. Ironically, he turns 20 today, following a knock yesterday that can only be described as a coming-of-age. If Fakhar was Pakistan’s anti-thesis to not showing up when it matters, Saad was the anti-thesis to a star performing batter never having enough support on the other end. “I have played domestic cricket with Saad, he is a very talented player,” Fakhar said, adding that Saad briskly scoring runs when he came to the crease yesterday allowed Fakhar to settle and take his time, and ultimately go big. “The credit goes to him for starting the way he did.” “Obviously there is pressure on you whenever you move to international cricket,” said Saad in a video reflection posted on PCB’s social media handles. “But the way you have to play through the pressure and back yourself, I was lacking that in the first two or three games, and was getting out in the 30s,” he added, saying that his plan for yesterday’s innings was to score while staying settled at the crease, and Fakhar’s “outstanding” innings made doing that all the more easier. He rotated strike and got into a good groove with Fakhar, rotating strike and picking out the Sri Lankan bowlers whenever the opportunity came to him. Perhaps the way he got out - an anticlimactic chip back to the bowler on a full Theekshana delivery - reflects where he stands in his career compared to the man across the other end, lacking just the final bit of grit and presence that can only come with time. And if these two left-handers set Pakistan on for victory, another one entirely made sure he finished it. Between overs 32.5 and 42.5, Pakistan did not score a single boundary. Fakhar and Salman Ali Agha had been bowled in quick succession. With Hasan Nawaz and Arafat new on the crease, and most of the toe-end of the innings left to bat through, their game plan seemed simple enough: don’t throw it away. The scoring during those overs came entirely from rotating strike, which might have felt grinding and underwhelming for an audience who had just witnessed a Fakhar Zaman special. Arafat Minhas plays a shot during the tri-nation series final at the Gaddafi Stadium, Lahore, on Saturday, 31st October 2026.–AFP It was a full Asitha Fernando delivery in the 45th over, drilled disdainfully down the ground, that would open the floodgates. In the bowler’s next over, Arafat hit possibly the cleanest, most sublime sequence of shots he has procured in his short career so far, bludgeoning two sixes and a four before holing out with Pakistan just two short of the win. “When I went in [to bat], I told Hasan that we have been through this situation before, and so we tried building a partnership,” he said. The two had carried out a deftly executed rescue job in their first tri-series fixture against England as well, ensuring Pakistan posted a total north of 300. “We backed each other and waited for bad balls to come to us.” “And I think through communicating with each other we had developed confidence in one another as well,” he said. Arafat was awarded player of the series as well - the second time he’s been awarded the title in as many ODI series he has participated in. “I have been saying from the beginning that I am an all-rounder,” he said in the ceremony. He was, after all, the leading architect with both bat and ball in Pakistan’s first win against England. “There is pressure, but the way you enjoy the pressure, stay calm during it, and execute your skills is important,” he said of the tricky place the team found itself in when he came in to bat with Hasan. Pakistan’s ODI assignments now all build up to the big shot at the big prize, the World Cup in South Africa next year. Young talents like Saad and Arafat is blooding in, and stalwarts like Fakhar hoping to find one final burst for the nation. What Pakistan can hope to take to South Africa is a team that sports both, the best of its recent past, and the most promising of its hopefully long future. And three left-handers on Saturday night in Lahore, showed exactly how to do it.

PIA's first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner arrives in Islamabad. Pakistan International Airlines’ (PIA) first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, acquired on lease last month, arrived in Islamabad from London as flight PK786 on Sunday. A PIA spokesperson, in a statement, said that the carrier is the first Pakistani airline to have added a Boeing 787-9 to its fleet. PIA Chief Executive Aamir Hayat, accompanied by his team, welcomed the Dreamliner at Islamabad airport, according to the statement. The plane is equipped with modern technology, including in-flight entertainment, and features a spacious and comfortable cabin, PIA said. “The inclusion of the Dreamliner is part of a strategy to modernise PIA’s fleet and strengthen its international network,” the spokesperson said. Photo shows the inside of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, which arrived in Islamabad on Sunday. — Photo courtesy PIA “PIA’s objective is to provide international-standard travel facilities and a more comfortable air travel experience to passengers through modern aircraft.” The Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner is a long-range, twin-engine plane with up to 325 seats. Previously, PIA’s fleet consisted of 12 Boeing 777 jets, 15 Airbus A320 planes and five smaller ATRs. Photo shows the inside of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, which arrived in Islamabad on Sunday. — Photo courtesy PIA Last month, PIA signed an ACMI (aircraft, crew, maintenance, and insurance) lease agreement with Norse Atlantic Airways to acquire two state-of-the-art Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners, one of which arrived in Islamabad on Sunday. A PIA spokesperson at the time said the addition of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner would mark the start of the airline’s expansion. By expanding its fleet, the airline aims to meet rising demand with direct flights and broader global connectivity, he added. The aircraft would operate direct long-haul flights from Pakistan to the United Kingdom, he said, adding that they would support PIA operations between different points in the UK and Pakistan. The development also comes as the government in September clarified that it was not buying any aircraft for the former national carrier after reports emerged of a federal minister arranging and negotiating sovereign-linked financing for PIA jets. PIA was privatised in December last year through an auction. A consortium led by Arif Habib Corporation Limited had won the auction for 75 per cent shares of PIA in December last year, making a winning bid of Rs135 billion. The Arif Habib-led consortium had vowed to transform the loss-making airline through operational restructuring, fleet expansion, and improved customer service.

Upper Dir police claim arresting 5 suspects over alleged assault of minor boy. LOWER DIR: Police in Upper Dir said on Sunday they have arrested five of the six suspects over the alleged assault and intimidation of a teenage boy, a purported video of which was circulated on social media. Wari Circle Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) Fakhr-i-Alam confirmed the arrests to Dawn . The incident took place on Oct 25, according to a first information report (FIR), dated Oct 30 and seen by Dawn , filed by Wari police on the boy’s complaint. The case invoked Sections 364-A (kidnapping or abducting an underage person), 342 (punishment for wrongful confinement), 506 (criminal intimidation), 147 (rioting) and 149 (unlawful assembly) of the Pakistan Penal Code . In the FIR, the boy alleged that on the day of the incident, a friend of his called him to a place where two men, including an unidentified tehsildar, forcibly made him board a car and took him to an under-construction house in Shinkarai. There, he was allegedly assaulted and threatened by the two men who demanded an “unnatural” act. The FIR nominated a total of six people, including his friend. Those arrested excluded one of the two men who made the boy board the car. The boy alleged that the two men who forced him into the car and three others present at the house kept him confined in a room for around three hours. The complainant further alleged that the two men who brought him there and another person recorded the incident on their mobile phones, while two others delivered blows to him with kicks, punches, and sticks. “Due to their blows, I sustained severe pain in my right shin, right and left arms, and across the rest of my body,” the boy said in the FIR. The complainant further claimed that the incident stemmed from WhatsApp conversations among friends. According to the complainant, the delay in reporting the incident was due to death threats from the suspects, who had also threatened to share the video. The video, reportedly recorded by some of the suspects, surfaced on social media days after the alleged incident, prompting police to take action. The allegations levelled in the FIR have yet to be independently verified by Dawn . Police said they had initiated an investigation into the case. Child protection NGO Sahil estimates that at least 558 cases of child abductions were reported across the country in the first six months of 2026.
