His death marks a major loss for the Polisario. The Moroccan strike came as UN envoy Staffan De Mistura was visiting the Tindouf refugee camps for consultations with the Polisario. Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani says this latest episode shows that negotiations to resolve the Western Sahara conflict are under increasing strain. The Polisario and its ally Algeria have routinely rejected framework agreements based on Morocco’s autonomy plan as other deadly attacks have eroded trust between the parties. 5 June 2026 COLOMBIA Far-right presidential candidate Abelardo de la Espriella won a first-round victory in the 31 May elections, setting up a 21 June run-off against left-wing senator Iván Cepeda. Cepeda promises to reduce inequality and continue talks with armed groups, while de la Espriella advocates iron-fist policies, including bombing organised crime groups, building mega-jails and restoring traditional values. After the vote, President Gustavo Petro alleged irregularities, despite international observers calling the vote transparent, while U.S. President Donald Trump openly backed de la Espriella. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says Petro’s claims raise concerns over a peaceful transfer of power if Cepeda loses, while Trump’s involvement has fuelled resentment over foreign interference, which could further trigger demonstrations. The run-off could also test whether Trump’s endorsement helps or hurts candidates elsewhere in the region. CONFLICT-RELATED SEXUAL VIOLENCE The UN on 29 May released its annual report on conflict-related sexual violence, showing that reported cases more than doubled in 2025 after rising 25 per cent the year before. UN Women also recently reported that in Sudan alone, the number of women and girls needing support after sexual violence has quadrupled since civil war broke out three years ago. Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing says survivor services are increasingly scarce after major U.S. aid cuts in 2025 hit programming for which Washington had been the largest donor. Compounding the problem, Washington’s February 2026 “Protecting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance” policy restricts aid recipients’ work and speech on abortion. Though the policy’s ban on “promoting” abortion exempts cases of rape, many NGOs fear inconsistent enforcement and unclear compliance requirements, leaving them to choose between U.S. conditions that may limit post-rape care and refusing funding at the risk of jeopardising their wider operations. LEBANON Israel and Lebanon on Wednesday agreed to a new U.S.-brokered ceasefire deal, which would establish pilot zones in southern Lebanon where Hizbollah operatives would be barred. The deal follows a severe Israeli escalation, including its deepest incursion into Lebanese territory in 26 years, which threatened to upset ongoing U.S.-Iran talks. The ceasefire depends on Hizbollah halting attacks and withdrawing fighters from south of the Litani River to allow the Lebanese army to assume control there. On Thursday, Hizbollah rejected the terms, after Israel said it would continue military operations for now. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the “pilot zones” proposal could offer a pragmatic way to address the parties’ security concerns. Unless Israel and Hizbollah both cease fire, however, this latest agreement will soon collapse entirely. 29 May 2026 GAZA Nickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat tasked by the U.S.-designed Board of Peace with overseeing the Gaza ceasefire, briefed the UN Security Council last week on his team’s first six months of work. He was upbeat, releasing a fifteen-point “roadmap” for the next stage. But conditions remain dire on the ground. Israel’s siege is tightening, meaning that reconstruction is impossible. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday he has ordered the Israeli army to increase the proportion of Gaza it controls from 60 to 70 per cent, in effect squeezing the strip’s two million people into an even tighter corner. Israeli airstrikes have taken more than 900 Palestinian lives during the ceasefire, including the commander of Hamas’s armed wing and, only days later, his successor, who was killed Wednesday along with his family. Israeli media reported that the Board of Peace had “approved” the assassinations. Crisis Group expert Max Rodenbeck says the Board’s strategy of making relief for Gaza’s people, whether humanitarian aid or broader hopes for the future, conditional on Hamas’s willingness to surrender its arms is deeply troubling and a recipe for prolonging their misery. KOREAN PENINSULA Pyongyang said it tested two new missiles Tuesday, including a short-range, nuclear-capable cruise missile that it plans to deploy with troops facing South Korean soldiers across the Korean peninsula’s demilitarised zone. The same day, Seoul said it had also detected North Korean missile launches toward waters off the peninsula’s western coast. Crisis Group expert Chris Green says the advanced weapon tests will deepen the freeze in peninsular relations, with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un branding South Korea his country’s foremost enemy and pledging to make the border “an impregnable fortress”. Along with Pyongyang’s growing closeness to Moscow and questions about Washington’s commitment to defending South Korea amid its mounting competition with Beijing, the tests are likely to bolster the consensus in Seoul behind more intensive military modernisation of its own. MALI As many as 50 people were killed Wednesday in jihadist raids on two villages in the central Mopti region, underscoring the breadth of the threat posed by the al-Qaeda affiliate Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM). Meanwhile, JNIM continued to enforce a partial siege of the capital Bamako, preventing scores of trucks bearing fuel and other supplies from reaching the city. In the north, Malian forces have stepped up airstrikes on Kidal and surrounding areas following the major offensive launched on 25 April by JNIM and northern separatist groups. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says these developments show that weapons continue to do the talking in Mali, even as the situation points to the urgent need for a genuine political dialogue. 22 May 2026 AFGHANISTAN Together with various NGOs, the UN released a plan Tuesday for aiding Afghan refugees expected to return from Iran and Pakistan in the coming months. The UN projects that 2.7 million people will cross back into Afghanistan between April and December. Already, nearly 5.9 million refugees have come back since September 2023, many of them forced to do so by harsh Pakistani visa policies amid rising tensions between Islamabad and the Taliban authorities in Kabul. Now the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will likely compel many Afghans living in the Islamic Republic to leave, even as the exodus from Pakistan continues. Many of these people are women, who will face draconian Taliban restrictions on freedom of movement and economic activity. The returnees also include children, some of whom have never even been to Afghanistan and will be at greater risk of child marriage, which the Taliban have lately recognised as a legal act. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says international donors should give generously to fund the $529 million UN response plan, without which many returnees will be destitute. NIGERIA The military announced Tuesday that joint strikes carried out with the U.S. had killed 175 jihadist fighters in the preceding week, in addition to destroying stockpiles of arms. The strikes began on 16 May with one that killed Abu Bakr al-Mainuki, deputy leader of the Islamic State-West Africa Province (ISWAP), who had been coordinating activities with jihadists in the Sahelian countries. At a hearing in Washington on Tuesday, General Dagvin Anderson, head of U.S. Africa Command, told U.S. legislators that “the epicentre of global terrorism is in Africa”. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says the latest operations underscore that Nigerian-U.S. security cooperation is deeper than Abuja and Washington had indicated earlier. They are a setback for ISWAP, at least for the time being. U.S. - CUBA The U.S. indicted former Cuban leader Raúl Castro Wednesday for murder and conspiring to kill U.S. nationals. The charges relate to a 1996 incident in which Cuban fighter jets shot at planes flown by anti-Castro Cuban Americans trying to help Cubans escape the island. These legal developments arrive amid renewed speculation that the Trump administration intends to decapitate the Cuban regime much as it did the Venezuelan government with its raid to snatch former President Nicolás Maduro in early January. Senior U.S. officials, most recently Central Intelligence Agency head John Ratcliffe, have held a series of semi-secret meetings with high-ranking figures in Havana this spring. Publicly, Cuban leader Miguel Díaz-Canel has remained defiant, rejecting the allegations against Castro as a “political manoeuvre”. Meanwhile, the U.S. has tightened a blockade of Cuba that has precipitated a humanitarian crisis and sent additional warships to the Caribbean Sea. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says any attempt to forcibly break the tight grip the Cuban Communist Party and military have upon the state could result in violent chaos and further suffering for the Cuban people. 15 May 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO A spate of lethal violence in the north-eastern Ituri province over the past two weeks has underscored the complexity of the country’s crisis. In late April, a group of Codeco militiamen killed at least 69 people, mainly civilians, in a series of separate attacks. Allied with the Congolese government, Codeco claims to defend the interests of the Lendu people, most of whom are farmers, from encroachment by ethnic Hema herders. According to local sources, it raided several Hema villages in retaliation for assaults on Congolese army positions by a Hema armed group. The following week, gunmen from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), a Ugandan insurgency now affiliated with the Islamic State, killed at least fifteen people in Biakato, an Ituri market town. The province has been under martial law since 2021, the same year that Uganda (with Kinshasa’s permission) sent in troops to pursue ADF militants based in Congolese territory. Crisis Group expert Onesphore Sematumba says the latest killings demonstrate the inadequacy of a purely military response to insecurity stemming from inter-communal tensions, competition for natural resources, state weakness and other causes. DISPLACEMENT A new report from the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre shows that armed conflict has become the number-one cause of internal displacement worldwide, surpassing natural disasters, for the first time on record. War and violence drove some 32.3 million people from their homes in 2025, the most ever, representing a 60 per cent increase over 2024. The internal displacements in Iran and the Democratic Republic of Congo made up two thirds of the global total. Crisis Group President and CEO Comfort Ero says these numbers are a sobering reminder of how pervasive conflict has become in today’s world. The human cost of war is never abstract. Preventing war means not just saving lives but also sparing people the pain and distress of being uprooted, often with no certainty of ever going home. U.S. - CHINA U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping concluded their long-awaited summit Friday. Crisis Group experts Ali Wyne and William Yang say it produced no major breakthrough, such as a joint commitment to de-escalate the conflict in the Middle East and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Nor did it bring a major reversal, which some in Taiwan had feared, such as Trump agreeing to scale back U.S. arms sales or change Washington’s longstanding declaratory policies toward the island. The summit was nonetheless illuminating in two respects. First, it underscored Trump’s desire to gain a greater foothold in China for U.S. businesses as well as his conviction that a strong working rapport with Xi can produce a cooperative relationship between Washington and Beijing. Secondly, it showcased how significantly China’s power and confidence have grown since Trump last visited China in November 2017. 8 May 2026 CAMBODIA - THAILAND The Thai cabinet voted Tuesday to cancel a 2001 memorandum of understanding with Cambodia on overlapping claims in the Gulf of Thailand. The agreement had provided for delimitation of maritime zones and joint development of hydrocarbon reserves in a portion of the 26,000 sq km overlapping claims area. Yet, in the 25 years since they signed it, the two countries have neither undertaken such projects nor resolved their territorial dispute. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, who campaigned on scrapping the document arguing that it had failed to achieve its objectives, insists that the decision is unrelated to tensions with Cambodia following border clashes in 2025. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says the cancellation will please Thai nationalists who have long alleged that the agreement placed Bangkok at a disadvantage, despite its language saying it is “without prejudice to the maritime claims of either party”. Cambodia expressed regret at Thailand’s action and said it plans to initiate compulsory conciliation, a non-binding dispute resolution mechanism under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. ETHIOPIA A showdown may be looming in Tigray, Ethiopia’s northernmost region, after its ruling party reinstated a state council Tuesday that was dissolved immediately before the bloody 2020-2022 Tigray war. The council was originally elected in 2020, in defiance of the federal government’s wishes. Addis Ababa installed a regional administration of its own choosing following the war, which Tigray’s ruling party has now, in effect, deposed. All eyes are now on the federal government, says Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor, watching for how it will respond. It has already imposed what amounts to an economic siege on Tigray, blocking fuel supplies and withholding budget subsidies. It may simply tighten these measures. Or it may intervene militarily to reinstate an Addis Ababa-aligned administration. A new conflict in Tigray could drag in neighbouring countries, particularly Eritrea, adding to the turmoil in the Horn of Africa, as Addis Ababa and Asmara appear to be aligning with different sides in Sudan’s civil war. U.S. - CHINA Chinese leader Xi Jinping is due to host U.S. President Donald Trump in Beijing next week for a long-awaited summit, which had been slated for the end of March. Crisis Group experts Ali Wyne and William Yang say trade will likely feature high on the agenda, with both men aiming to maintain the tariff truce they reached last year. The Middle East conflict – which caused the delay – will also loom large, and both will seek to use it for leverage. The U.S. has sanctioned five Chinese oil refiners and accused China of “funding the largest state sponsor of terrorism” as it maintains a naval blockade of Iran. But Washington needs Chinese gallium to replenish its stockpile of missile interceptors in the Middle East, and it may need Beijing’s help to get Tehran back to the negotiating table. In exchange, Xi may try to extract security concessions from Trump, perhaps by asking him to lessen U.S. defence backing for Taiwan or to declare that the U.S. “opposes“ (rather than “does not support“, which is the longstanding U.S. position) Taiwanese independence. 1 May 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Fresh violence between Afghanistan and Pakistan erupted this week. Afghan authorities said Pakistani mortars and missiles hit a university and residential neighbourhoods in eastern Kunar province on Monday, killing at least seven people and wounding at least 85. Pakistan denied targeting civilians, saying its strikes aimed at militants, based on intelligence. Pakistani officials accused Afghan forces of cross-border attacks as well, including mortar fire at Chaman and South Waziristan, which they said killed several civilians and injured others. The exchanges followed China-mediated talks in April, during which the two sides agreed to explore a diplomatic solution to their dispute. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says mutual partners, particularly China, should urge both sides to de-escalate tensions, including through an agreed-upon oversight mechanism, to prevent the situation from deteriorating further. COLOMBIA Nearly two dozen people are dead and scores injured after a series of apparently coordinated attacks in the country’s south west that authorities blamed on Estado Mayor Central (EMC), a dissident faction of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia. Militants used drones, explosives and roadblocks to hit targets including police stations and military bases. On 25 April, improvised explosive devices went off on a major highway in Cauca, striking a bus and other civilian vehicles, killing at least twenty. The preceding a day, a bus full of explosives detonated near a major military base in Cali, Colombia's third-largest city. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the wave of violence indicates EMC’s capacity to disrupt daily life and terrorise civilians. Colombia's next president, to be elected on 31 May, will need to take urgent steps to better protect civilians. MALI On Saturday, the al-Qaeda affiliate Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, alongside separatists from the Azawad Liberation Front in northern Mali, assailed seven Malian cities, including the capital Bamako. Militants struck the garrison at Kati, less than 20km from Bamako, often described as the centre of military power, where they assassinated the defence minister and reportedly wounded other regime figures. They also retook the northern city of Kidal, the symbolic seat of the separatist movement, before negotiating the departure of Russian paramilitaries and Malian troops. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jézéquel says these attacks mark a new stage in Mali’s decades-long jihadist insurgency, characterised by increased pressure on urban areas, aimed at weakening and delegitimising state authority. 24 April 2026 JAPAN On Monday, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s cabinet lifted restrictions on the export of lethal weapons, allowing Japan to sell arms to seventeen countries with which it has defence transfer agreements. Tokyo first limited such transactions in 1967 and instituted a near total ban in 1976. It will continue to bar arms exports to countries at war, but exceptions may be granted. Meanwhile, last Saturday Beijing said two Chinese navy ships had transited waters between Japan’s Amami Oshima and Yokoate islands for exercises in the western Pacific. The announcement came one day before Japanese combat troops joined the annual Philippine-U.S. Balikatan exercise for the first time. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says these developments illustrate the accelerating defence modernisation in the Asia Pacific in response to what U.S.-allied countries perceive as Beijing’s coercive behaviour and uncertainty about Washington’s ability to sustain strategic focus on the region. ROHINGYA Nearly 900 Rohingya refugees died or were reported missing while trying to make perilous sea crossings in 2025, the UN said last week. It is the highest number ever, representing one in seven of the Rohingya who braved such journeys. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says this grim record points to the increasing desperation among the Rohingya in camps in southern Bangladesh, who are facing cuts to food aid. Unable to go home to Myanmar’s Rakhine State, which is wracked by war, or to work legally in Bangladesh, ever more refugees are trying to escape by boat to Malaysia, Thailand or Indonesia. The new Bangladeshi government should permit Rohingya to secure jobs in sectors with labour shortages. The more ways the Rohingya have to earn a living in refuge, the fewer of them will risk their lives at sea. U.S. - IRAN President Donald Trump announced an indefinite extension of the ceasefire in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran Tuesday, though keeping the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports in place. Iran tightened its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz Wednesday, firing on two cargo vessels attempting passage. Negotiations in Pakistan seem to be on hold, with conflicting signals about whether Tehran will send a delegation. With major combat on pause, say Crisis Group experts Michael Wahid Hanna and Ali Vaez, both sides are seeking to gain the upper hand through economic disruption – Washington by tightening its financial squeeze on the Islamic Republic and Tehran by prolonging the uncertainty in global markets. Both can keep inflicting pain, but their game of chicken could escalate into renewed hostilities at any time. Meanwhile, it adds yet another impediment to resuming talks. 17 April 2026 LIBYA The rival Tripoli and Benghazi-based legislative bodies approved a U.S.-mediated unified budget Saturday. The first such budget in more than thirteen years, it consolidates public spending throughout the country within a single framework. The budget’s passage coincided with the launch of the U.S.-led Flintlock 26 special forces joint training exercise in Sirte, bringing together Libya's two rival military coalitions alongside troops from the U.S., Italy and ten African nations. Crisis Group expert Claudia Gazzini says both initiatives are part of Washington's effort to bridge the gap between the country's two governments and their respective leading families: the Haftars in the east and the Dabaibas in the west. Many Libyans remain sceptical of moves that entrench the two families' authority, however, and wary of a budget deal that sounds promising but whose details have yet to be made public. SOUTH SUDAN Opposition forces this week retook the strategic town of Akobo in Jonglei state after government troops withdrew. Akobo is one of the last strongholds of fighters loyal to Vice President Riek Machar, whom President Salva Kiir’s government detained and put on trial last year. The army had seized the town in March. The fighting comes amid mounting warnings from the UN and aid organisations about deteriorating humanitarian conditions in Jonglei, where both sides stand accused of blocking aid access and displacing hundreds of thousands of civilians through sweeping evacuation orders. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the conflict shows no sign of abating. The toll of hostilities is already severe. Without stronger external pressure for de-escalation, conditions are likely to worsen. UKRAINE Russia launched over 600 drones and dozens of missiles at Ukrainian cities early Thursday, reportedly killing eighteen people, one of its deadliest air raids on Ukraine this year. Moscow said the barrage was retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on energy and military facilities. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who visited Germany, Norway and Italy this week seeking more air defence systems, has warned that Ukraine faces a severe shortage of the Patriot interceptors needed to fend off Russian ballistic missiles. As the war in the Middle East further depletes global interceptor stocks, Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says Ukraine will become increasingly vulnerable to Russian aerial attack. 10 April 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Afghanistan and Pakistan agreed Wednesday not to escalate their conflict further but to persevere at dialogue, following mediation by China. Fighting between the two countries has killed hundreds and displaced almost 100,000 since late February. Cross-border fire also cut the supply routes to some 100,000 people in Afghanistan’s Nuristan province, leaving them unable to receive the humanitarian aid they need. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says the continued talks are a positive sign. It remains to be seen, however, if Kabul and Islamabad can reach a sustainable settlement that includes verification mechanisms. IRAN The U.S. and Iran agreed Wednesday to a two-week ceasefire in the war that began on 28 February, with negotiations starting Friday in the Pakistani capital. The truce has been honoured in the breach, however, with Israel continuing to bomb Lebanon, Iran hitting Gulf Arab states and commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remaining suppressed. President Donald Trump underscored that the U.S. military is poised to resume hostilities if diplomatic efforts fail. After the fog of war comes the smog of ceasefire, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez. The parties have different interpretations of the ceasefire’s terms and are sticking to maximalist negotiating positions as the high-stakes talks in Islamabad commence. LEBANON On Wednesday, Israel carried out its heaviest airstrikes in Lebanon since its latest war with Hizbollah began on 2 March, killing more than 300 people and injuring over a thousand in just 24 hours. The strikes, which Israel claims aimed to knock out Hizbollah assets, hit densely populated areas in Beirut, the Bekaa valley and southern Lebanon. On Thursday and Friday, Israel launched another 50 air raids, killing at least seventeen more people. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the U.S. and European countries should put concerted pressure on Israel to extend the two-week ceasefire to Lebanon. Since Hizbollah entered the Middle East war, Israeli bombardment has killed more than 1,530 people, including 130 children, and displaced roughly one in every five Lebanese. 3 April 2026 HAITI Fresh gang violence struck central Haiti after the Gran Grif gang attacked Jean-Denis in Petite-Rivière de l’Artibonite, a stronghold of community defence groups, on Sunday. Its assaults went on for days, reportedly killing at least 70 people and displacing around 9,000. On Tuesday, Gran Grif reportedly joined another gang, Kokorat San Ras, in seizing parts of nearby Marchand-Dessalines. The flare-up coincides with the arrival of the first Chadian troops under the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, as Kenyan officers who served in the Multinational Security Support mission begin to withdraw. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the attacks show that gangs remain entrenched despite having scaled back their activity in recent months. They control most of the capital Port-au-Prince and are likely assessing their next moves outside it. Haitian security forces must stand ready during the high-risk period ahead. Gangs could go on the offensive as the Kenya-led mission phases out and the new force takes over. IRAN In a speech Wednesday evening, President Donald Trump said the U.S. would hit Iran “extremely hard”, sending it “back to the Stone Age” by bombing power plants if Tehran does not acquiesce to U.S. terms for ending the war. He also claimed such a deal was nearing completion. Washington has meanwhile deployed thousands more troops in the region, while Iran has continued attacks on Israel and Gulf Arab neighbours. Tehran has also kept a stranglehold on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, as Yemen’s Houthis warn that further escalation could prompt them to close the Bab al-Mandab, increasing the strain on maritime traffic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says a month of U.S.-Israeli strikes have brought the Iranian regime no closer to capitulation. So long as Washington and Tehran are pressing maximalist demands, believing they can force the other to yield, the war risks getting worse. SYRIA Sectarian unrest erupted in the predominantly Christian town of Suqaylabiyah in western Syria last Saturday. An argument over allegations of harassment reportedly prompted hundreds of men from the neighbouring Sunni-majority town of Qalaat al-Madiq to rush into Suqaylabiyah, ransacking Christian shops, homes and other property. Clashes lasted for hours until government forces brought in reinforcements to restore order. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the episode underscores persistent shortcomings in Syria's security architecture. State forces tend to react to such incidents rather than help prevent them. Largely drawn from the Sunni majority, these forces lack understanding of minority groups, whose trust in the new authorities is fast eroding. Until the government addresses those weaknesses, the risk of more such violence will remain high – particularly in diverse areas where tensions built over fourteen years of war are still raw. 27 March 2026 IRAN With the Middle East war in its fourth week, the Trump administration submitted to Tehran, via Pakistani mediators, what U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff described as a “fifteen-point action list that forms the framework for a peace deal”. Meanwhile, the U.S. is sending more ground troops to the region. More likely is a protracted standoff or, worse, a dramatic escalation. IRAQ Fresh hostilities erupted this week between the U.S. and Iraqi militias backed by Tehran. These groups belong to an umbrella institution, the Hashd al-Shaabi, that is formally under the aegis of the Iraqi military commander-in-chief, though some of them operate independently. Those aligned with Iran have launched several rockets at U.S. bases in Iraq and neighbouring countries. A retaliatory U.S. airstrike on the Hashd headquarters in Baghdad killed fifteen fighters and another on a military facility in western Iraq claimed seven more lives. Meanwhile, the peshmerga in Iraqi Kurdistan, who are friendly to Washington, said Iranian missiles hit one of their bases in Erbil, killing six. The Iraqi government protested the infringements upon its sovereignty. But it lacks the leverage to stop the deadly exchanges, says Crisis Group expert Lahib Higel. SUDAN UN agencies issued statements Tuesday protesting a “sharp increase” in drone warfare that is taking a mounting civilian toll. At least 70 people were killed the previous day when drones hit a hospital in East Darfur. Patients, doctors and nurses were among the dead. Another 28 civilians were killed in drone strikes in North Darfur and North Kordofan Thursday. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says Chad, which hosts around one million Sudanese refugees, increasingly risks getting drawn into the war in Sudan as fighting routinely spills across the border. IRAN Oil and gas prices soared and stock markets dived Thursday after Iran struck Qatar’s main natural gas facility, Ras Laffan. NIGERIA Multiple suicide bombings Monday killed at least 26 people and injured over a hundred in Maiduguri, capital of Nigeria’s Borno state. It has also sent more troops into southern Lebanon, with a view to establishing what it calls a “security zone” there. On Wednesday, it launched a barrage of 100 rockets across the border, which triggered an especially brutal sequence of Israeli air raids. Crisis Group expert David Wood says neither of the belligerents appears ready to stop, even as Lebanese leaders scramble to find a diplomatic off-ramp. In retaliation, Iran fired missiles and drones at Israel, as well as U.S. bases and commercial infrastructure in Gulf states. The conflict's reverberations have quickly spread from the Indian Ocean to the eastern Mediterranean. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Tehran looks prepared for a drawn-out confrontation, betting that it can steadily raise the psychological and economic costs to its adversaries, while maintaining cohesion at the top of the political system despite Khamenei’s demise. AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Border clashes continued this week after Pakistan declared “open war” with Afghanistan last Friday. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. AFP / Ludovic Marin Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 23 October 2026 13 minutes How Algeria’s Rupture with the UAE Could Roil the Region Algiers has severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi, following years of discord over crises in North Africa and the Sahel. The two countries see their dispute very differently, but it has nonetheless become a rivalry that could put regional stability at risk. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Michaël Béchir Ayari Senior Analyst, Tunisia Related Tags Algeria United Arab Emirates On 10 September, Algeria broke off diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, in the latest manifestation of a confrontation between the two countries over policy in the Middle East, North Africa and the Sahel. Since 2020, disagreements have festered between Algiers and Abu Dhabi over Israel, Morocco and Western Sahara. Algeria has also grown increasingly suspicious of the aims of Emirati involvement in crises in Libya, Sudan and Sahelian states. The rupture is marked by an asymmetry of perceptions. Algiers sees the UAE, sitting far away in the Gulf, as interfering in its North African and Sahelian neighbourhood, where it is looking to rebuild the diplomatic clout that it wielded for decades after winning independence from French colonial rule in 1962. It views Emirati interventions as, at the very least, encroachments upon its historical domain. Abu Dhabi, for its part, says economic ties, not Algeria, are central to its African engagement. It forswears any intent to provoke or sideline Algiers. The bilateral discord has become a full-blown rivalry, however, and one that is becoming perilous as regional security arrangements are changing. Algeria is forging closer links with Niger, as well as with Chad. It is also backing the Sudanese army in its war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli in its power struggle with Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, whose forces control the country’s east . Algerian officials describe these moves as reinforcing the country’s “ strategic borders ”. Algeria remains bitterly at odds with Morocco over Western Sahara and other issues, and it is just now repairing relations with Mali. Meanwhile, the UAE is forming its own partnerships in North Africa and the Sahel, which can involve both states and armed groups, and which often (though not always) put it indirectly in competition with Algeria. A direct clash between the two countries is unlikely. Their respective alliance systems overlap somewhat and do not constitute coherent groups of adversaries. Still, jostling among them could draw in Algeria, the UAE or both, with the risk of local escalation or inadvertent confrontation. Roots of the Break-up Dramatic as the 10 September rupture was, it had been a long time coming. Until 2020, relations between Algeria and the UAE were strong. In the early 1970s, Algeria sent oil experts, including executives from Sonatrach, Algeria’s state-owned hydrocarbons company, to the Gulf to help establish the institutions that would become the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company. Abdelaziz Bouteflika, who served as Algeria’s president between 1999 and 2019, lived in Abu Dhabi from 1984 to 1987, working as a diplomatic adviser to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, father of today’s leader Mohammed bin Zayed (aka MBZ). During Bouteflika’s tenure as Algerian head of state, Emirati capital made significant inroads into the Algerian economy, including in the defence sector. In 2012, for example, Emirati investors cooperated with the Algerian defence ministry and state-owned companies in joint ventures to produce Mercedes-Benz vehicles and Emirati-designed NIMR armoured vehicles in Algeria. The UAE built networks of contacts within the Algerian political, business and military elite, some of which survived Bouteflika’s fall in 2019. The UAE’s 2020 normalisation with Israel – part of what is known as the Abraham Accords – opened a first crack in the relationship. Algiers firmly opposed any Arab state forging ties with Israel before a comprehensive settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In September 2020, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune criticised what he described as a “ rush ” ( empressement ) toward normalisation, declaring that Algeria would not be part of it. Algiers has long been the foremost outside backer of the Polisario Front, the group battling for an independent Western Sahara. Algerian concerns grew further when, on 4 November 2020, the UAE became the first Arab country to open a consulate in Western Sahara, establishing a diplomatic office in Laayoune, a city in the Moroccan-controlled part of the disputed territory. Algiers has long been the foremost outside backer of the Polisario Front, the group battling for an independent Western Sahara. Sabri Boukadoum, then Algeria’s foreign minister, questioned the move’s compatibility with international law and reaffirmed Algerian support for Sahrawi self-determination. A month later, Morocco followed the UAE in normalising relations with Israel, prompting Algerian authorities to discern an emerging UAE-Morocco-Israel alliance in their immediate vicinity. This perception was significantly reinforced in November 2021, when Morocco and Israel signed a landmark defence cooperation agreement . The agreement formalised defence ties and paved the way for cooperation in areas including intelligence and military training. Algerian authorities viewed this deepening partnership as tantamount to a direct threat , part of a regional alignment aimed at weakening their country. Algerian worries extended to allegations of foreign interference in domestic affairs. Officials accused Morocco and Israel of supporting the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylia (MAK) , an independence movement that Algeria designated a terrorist organisation in 2021. As evidence, they pointed to the fact that Morocco’s representative at the UN had publicly argued that the Kabyle people are entitled to exercise a right to self-determination . A number of former Algerian diplomats and commentators implicated the UAE in these purported destabilisation efforts as well: a Morocco-based think-tank separately reported on contacts between MAK representatives and Emirati figures, citing sources within the Kabyle independence movement, among others. The Dispute Deepens Other regional disagreements added to the tensions. In 2020 and again in 2022 , Abu Dhabi opposed the appointment of successive Algerian foreign ministers as UN envoys to Libya, against the backdrop of Emirati support for Field Marshal Haftar, and Algeria’s closer links with the authorities in Tripoli. The UAE cited the objections of Arab states and Libyan actors, expressing their concern that Algeria, as a neighbouring country deeply involved in the conflict, could not be viewed as an impartial mediator. Another friction point surfaced in 2023, when Algerian government-aligned media attributed the failure of Algeria’s BRICS application to Emirati manoeuvring against its candidacy. Views in Algiers on how to counter the UAE’s gambits – real and perceived – may not have been entirely aligned. Some elements of the security establishment and associated media favoured a confrontational approach, while others, including figures close to former army Chief of Staff Ahmed Gaïd Salah, worried about jeopardising significant economic interests and longstanding personal connections. The exact boundaries of these contrasting viewpoints, however, remained unclear. As Emirati actions increasingly clashed with Algeria’s regional priorities and came to be perceived as national security threats , displaying restraint became more difficult. Despite his initial reticence to comment on the matter, President Tebboune’s criticism of the UAE gradually became louder. Despite his initial reticence to comment on the matter, President Tebboune’s criticism of the UAE gradually became louder. In 2024, he complained that wherever conflict erupted in the region , the money of an unnamed Gulf state could be found behind it; in 2025, he said Algeria enjoyed good relations with all Gulf monarchies, except one . By the following February, he was openly denouncing a “ mini-state ” that was destabilising the Arab world and the Sahel. Successive attempts to ease tensions made little headway. Former Algerian diplomats told Crisis Group that Gulf states, including Bahrain and Oman, sent emissaries to Algiers to try mediating between the two sides. They said Algeria rejected these efforts, however, and will keep doing so as long as what it regards as Emirati meddling continues. Direct contacts endured, but they failed to achieve a thaw. By February, when Algeria terminated the 2013 bilateral agreement that provided the legal framework for air travel between the two countries, the room for compromise had considerably narrowed. Rivalry in the Sahel As relations deteriorated, the dispute increasingly spilled into a contest for influence in North Africa and the Sahel. A May 2024 tour of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso by UAE Minister of State Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan raised hackles in Algeria , which has long described Mali in particular as a “brother” nation. Abu Dhabi was offering the Sahelian capitals cooperation on counter-terrorism just as Western influence was waning in the region and the new Alliance of Sahel States (AES) was opening it to new external patrons. There were other angles as well: for the UAE, security cooperation is inseparable from economic interests, particularly when it comes to natural resources; Dubai’s role in the international gold trade, including gold originating in the Sahel, gave the UAE an additional stake in regional developments. Meanwhile, Algeria’s historical ties with Bamako and the other AES capitals were reaching a nadir. Emirati officials maintain that its engagement was not aimed at supplanting Algeria. Indeed, they rarely present Algiers as a competitor when discussing the Sahel or any other African region. Rather, they say, Abu Dhabi is pursuing a broad strategy, rooted in geo-economics , designed to expand the UAE’s footprint on a continent that has gained in importance. As an Emirati businessman and former government official told Crisis Group in explaining the scope of Abu Dhabi’s ambition, “You’re either at the table or on the menu”. Algerian officials, by contrast, view the UAE’s combination of investments and partnerships with governments, business elites and armed actors as a means of undermining their country’s interests. They regard the Sahel as crucial to Algerian security, particularly since Bamako abandoned the Algeria-mediated 2015 peace agreement with armed separatists in northern Mali, whom they fear could make common cause with co-ethnics on the Algerian side of the border. Algerian concerns were heightened by allegations of ransom payments , mentioned in an August UN report and linked to the UAE by regional sources , to the jihadist group JNIM that has grabbed chunks of Malian and other Sahelian state territory. Algiers has long argued that such payments strengthen armed groups active near its frontiers. The contrast in approach and threat perceptions became particularly acute over events in Niger. Following a 2023 coup there, relations between Algiers and Niamey soured, and they worsened further in April 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador from Algiers in solidarity with authorities in Bamako, with whom Algiers was then at loggerheads over the abrogated peace agreement and other issues. Bilateral ties subsequently improved, following Nigerien leader General Abdourahamane Tiani’s visit to Algiers the following February . The two countries revived their security cooperation, and Niger even helped broker the present rapprochement between Algeria and Mali. Relations with Niger ... have an important economic dimension for both Algeria and the UAE. Relations with Niger also have an important economic dimension for both Algeria and the UAE. Algeria considers Niger key to its effort to reconnect with sub-Saharan Africa through energy and trade. Its flagship project is the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline , intended to carry Nigerian gas through Niger into Algeria and onward to Europe. Here, the UAE has a competing interest: the Trans-Saharan route directly competes with Morocco’s Atlantic pipeline , which is expected to run along the West African coast and which the UAE has backed with early financing. It is against this backdrop that Algeria viewed a failed coup against Tiani on 29 August as threatening its interests. Rumours swirled in Algiers about an Emirati hand . To date, these are unsubstantiated, but they have only deepened suspicions regarding the UAE’s activities in the Sahel. Algeria responded to the coup attempt by deploying four Su-30MKA fighter jets to Niamey , accompanied by an Il-78 aerial-refuelling aircraft and an Il-76 transport plane. Algerian analysts told Crisis Group that mechanics, logistics specialists and personnel for force protection were also dispatched. Beyond sending a clear signal of support for Tiani’s government, these steps showcased Algeria’s determination to regain influence in a region where it has lost considerable ground – and where it appears to have identified the UAE as a chief antagonist. Algeria’s actions also embodied something more, again with implications for relations with the UAE: a shift away from its longstanding aversion to military operations abroad. Since independence, Algeria’s leaders have framed the country’s foreign policy around non-alignment, anti-imperialism, national sovereignty, diplomatic mediation, South-South solidarity, support for national liberation and self-determination movements, and, importantly, non-interference in other states’ domestic affairs. There have been exceptions, and Algeria has at times interpreted this last precept flexibly when it has felt that it has important interests at stake. Overall, however, reluctance to dispatch regular military forces abroad has remained a powerful institutional constraint. Only in 2020 did a constitutional amendment create a legal framework for overseas deployments. The latter still require parliamentary approval and are restricted to internationally sanctioned missions. More recently, the army’s top general Saïd Chengriha has promoted the concept that Algeria has “ strategic borders ”. Though it does not formally establish a right to military intervention in neighbouring countries, this notion expands Algeria’s security perimeter by treating instability, armed groups and trafficking networks beyond its frontiers as potential national security threats. Rivalry in North Africa and the Horn In other regional conflicts, Algeria and the UAE likewise stand on opposing sides. In Libya, Field Marshal Haftar’s forces have, over time, received extensive Emirati backing . In contrast, Algeria has stood with Tripoli (which itself has maintained tight relations with Niger). In Sudan, Algeria sides with the army, whose leaders it considers the country’s legitimate representatives; several Algerian analysts told Crisis Group that in 2025 Algiers discreetly provided the Sudanese army with equipment, including old Russian MiG-29 fighter jets and spare parts. By contrast, Abu Dhabi refers to the army-led administration as the “ Port Sudan authority ”, in reference to its erstwhile seat in Port Sudan, treating it merely as one party to the conflict; it is widely believed to be sending support to the army’s main adversary, the RSF, though the UAE denies the claim. The divergent policies toward Sudan have had wider repercussions. Eastern and southern Libya reportedly have served as logistical corridors for supplies to the RSF allegedly originating with the Emirates . Previously, much of this materiel allegedly went through eastern Chad. For its part, the UAE maintains that its activities in eastern Chad are humanitarian , particularly getting aid to Sudanese refugees. An Algerian expert told Crisis Group that policymakers in Algiers appear intent on deepening ties with N’Djamena at least in part to counterbalance what they view as Sudan-linked Emirati networks in Chad. That said, Chadian President Idriss Déby has invested considerable political capital in his relationship with the UAE, whose substantial financial support , including a $1.5 billion budget financing agreement signed in 2023, gives the latter sway that Algeria would struggle to match. The growing Algeria-UAE rivalry could deepen existing Libyan divisions and turn local disputes into arenas of indirect regional confrontation. These competing relationships run the risk of reinforcing regional divisions, with Field Marshal Haftar and Chad being generally close to Abu Dhabi, while Tripoli and Niger cooperate more with Algiers. Conversely, the growing Algeria-UAE rivalry could deepen existing Libyan divisions and turn local disputes into arenas of indirect regional confrontation. To some extent, it already has. In August 2024, for example, Haftar’s forces moved toward Ghadames, only a few kilometres from the Algerian frontier, a development Algiers saw as threatening. The crisis eventually subsided after Haftar’s spokesman denied that the city was a military objective and insisted that the border with Algeria was secure . Still, the episode reinforced perceptions in Algiers of a UAE-backed menace in its neighbourhood. Tensions continue to build. Algeria is increasingly concerned by Haftar’s influence in southern Libya, where his forces have tightened their grip on lucrative trafficking routes and strengthened cooperation with N’Djamena in fighting Chadian rebel groups. Haftar has thus obtained access to an important source of income and displaced Chadian rebels toward northern Niger, particularly the strategic Salvador Pass area , exacerbating instability near Algeria’s southern border. All in all, these developments help explain Algeria’s evolving approach to regional security. Rather than viewing events in Libya, Niger and Sudan separately, Algiers increasingly sees them as interconnected challenges. Containing the Clash What began as a downturn in Algerian-UAE relations has thus evolved into a full-blown crisis with possible reverberations across the northern third of Africa. Algeria has remained silent as to why precisely it severed diplomatic ties. The foreign ministry’s statement was vague , referring to “provocative or hostile” actions as well as warnings that had failed to deter Abu Dhabi from unspecified behaviour. Algeria may have avoided identifying grievances or conditions for reconciliation in order to allow for flexibility in future talks. The difficulty of substantiating its complaints may also have contributed to its ambiguous stance. To officials in Abu Dhabi, the break was both unanticipated and perplexing. Though he did not name Algeria, Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, alluded to it in a tweet complaining of “ puzzles and signals that require decoding ” in interstate relations. The UAE foreign ministry adopted a more conciliatory tone, expressing hope that the rupture would prove temporary. A number of Emirati analysts said the dispute is of far greater significance to Algeria than to the UAE, given Abu Dhabi’s preoccupation with the war in the Gulf. These reactions underscore a divergence in perspectives: while Algiers views Abu Dhabi’s alliances as a growing threat to its regional influence, Abu Dhabi sees its engagement as part of a strategy driven by political, economic and security interests that go beyond any bilateral relationship. In reality, neither country can bar the other from an ever more cutthroat arena. Too, governments and armed groups in the region cannot be neatly categorised into two rival blocs; each of Niger, Chad and the assorted Libyan players has its own agenda that may not align precisely with either Algerian or Emirati wishes. Still, as Algeria assumes a more assertive stance and the UAE pursues its geographically expansive approach, seemingly oblivious to, or at least underestimating the depth of Algeria’s concerns and its conviction that Abu Dhabi is challenging its position, bilateral tensions risk becoming more fraught. Informal communication channels could help shed light on their respective intentions and minimise the chance of misinterpretation and accidental conflict. The two countries would be far better served by taking steps and shifting their mindsets to help ensure that Emirati influence in Algeria’s neighbourhood, and Algiers’ response to it, do not become a trigger for bilateral confrontation. First, though full reconciliation may be out of reach for the moment, maintaining or restoring informal communication channels could help shed light on their respective intentions and minimise the chance of misinterpretation and accidental conflict. Secondly, Algiers should avoid construing every Emirati undertaking in neighbouring countries as part of a strategy directed against its interests. Finally, Abu Dhabi ought to take Algeria’s security concerns more seriously. It should recognise that its regional partnerships, particularly those involving armed non-state actors, may threaten Algerian interests, even when not so intended. Both countries should have an interest in preventing local disputes from drawing them further toward confrontation, particularly given that both neighbouring governments and armed groups pursue agendas neither side can fully control. Absent such efforts, the rift could deepen, increasing the risk that local crises spiral into open hostility. The result would be to exacerbate tensions in a region already riven by deadly conflict. Syria's New Reconstruction Fund a Chance for Reform. Click to expand Image An aerial view of a damaged area of Damascus where the debris from collapsed buildings is being turned into sand, gravel, and bricks to reuse as construction materials to restore areas affected by Syria’s civil war, November 2, 2025. © 2025 Bakr Al Kasem/Anadolu via Getty Images Syria and the World Bank Group announced on October 18 the creation of the Syria Recovery and Reconstruction Trust Fund, known as START. Run by the World Bank, the fund will pool donor money and private investment to help restore infrastructure and public services, strengthen state institutions, and finance reforms the Syrian government identifies as priorities. The World Bank estimates Syria’s post-conflict reconstruction will cost about US$216 billion. Norway pledged approximately 90 million krone ($9.6 million) and the Netherlands €15 million ($16.8 million). START’s initial focus, according to Syria’s state news agency, SANA, is infrastructure, health and education. It will operate under World Bank policies, which include standards on stakeholder engagement, land acquisition, and grievance mechanisms. But those standards only cover START-funded projects and governance arrangements are still being finalized, according to SANA. The moment offers a chance to strengthen protections for Syria’s wider reconstruction, beyond START’s projects. Current rules governing reconstruction do not require consultation with affected communities, including tenants, informal occupants, and displaced people before projects are approved, and there is no specialized mechanism for reconstruction disputes. The consequences of policies that are implemented without consulting those most affected are already evident: In March, local authorities in Damascus proposed giving foreign companies land in Jobar and Qaboun in exchange for financing and building a reconstruction project. Owners of homes in zoned areas would get new units half the size of their old ones. Owners of land in informal settlements would get only 30 percent of their land. And the plan made no provision for tenants. The World Bank and START's donors should make a rights-aligned framework for housing, land, and property a priority among the reforms the fund supports, including an independent property dispute mechanism. They should require human rights impact assessments before funding projects with unresolved property claims. They should prioritize restoring services where people are returning. And any support for private health or education providers should carry enforceable requirements on affordability, quality, and nondiscrimination. Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh says the priority now is “tangible results for the Syrian people.” The real test is whether those people have a say in decisions about their land and whether they can enjoy their rights to health, education, and housing.

Brazil: New Evidence of Serious Police Misconduct in Deadly Raid. Play Video Read a text description of this video TEXT ON SCREEN October 28, 2025 Rio de Janeiro, Brazil NARRATION On the morning of October 28th, 2025, hundreds of police officers surrounded two low-income neighborhoods in Rio de Janeiro. By nightfall, the operation would become the deadliest in Brazil's history. TEXT ON SCREEN WARNING. This video contains graphic content, including blurred images of dead bodies. Viewer discretion advised. NARRATION 122 people were killed, including two children and five police officers. According to the autopsy records, over eighty five percent of non-police victims were Black. Police in Rio de Janeiro are required by Supreme Court order to wear body cameras. However, only twenty-three percent of officers wore body cameras that day, and in the footage reviewed by Human Rights Watch, not a single killing was captured on camera. LOWER THIRD Damir Khairat Research Technologist Digital Investigations Lab NARRATION Human Rights Watch was given access to the prosecutor's investigation into the operation, including 8,800 pages of records, 122 autopsies, and nearly 4,000 hours of body camera footage. TEXT ON SCREEN Prosecutors have released the body camera footage shown in this video. Most footage is sealed as evidence and cannot be published. NARRATION Watching all the footage day and night without any breaks would have taken a single researcher almost six months. So, we trained several artificial intelligence models to help us identify the moments that mattered most. First, we needed to organize everything. The models, alongside software that Human Rights Watch developed, synchronized recordings from different officers, mapped their locations, and scanned footage for gunshots and signs of camera tampering. From there we had a searchable platform that let us view the operation as one coordinated event, rather than thousands of separate recordings. What we found was evidence of widespread tampering and obstruction of body cameras. And it consistently happened at the exact moment cameras should have been recording, during arrests, shootouts, or while officers entered homes. Authorities said that the purpose of the raid was to arrest suspected drug traffickers. The evidence we found points to an operation that appeared lethal by design. To explain how we came to this conclusion, let's look at some examples of the moments we trained our AI models to detect. An officer's camera captured this video in an alleyway as a large group of his colleagues pass by, after which the officer quickly covers his camera. He or another officer then flags that there's a camera recording. SOUNDBITE [IN PORTUGUESE] The team has a camera. The team has a camera. No, no I’m talking about the thing there. NARRATION It's unclear why he covered it, but prosecutors later charged him with camera tampering. SOUNDBITE So, this would be the kind of like overall operational view. NARRATION To find incidents like this across almost 4,000 hours of footage from nearly 500 officers, we trained a model to detect similar moments when a camera continued recording, but the lens was covered. Here, an officer is seen struggling to pick the lock on the door of someone's home. Once it's open, he removes his camera and leaves it unattended for over an hour, presumably while he's inside the home. Because the camera was still capturing an image, this recording wasn't initially flagged by our software. So, we trained a second model to identify "stale scenes" where the recording stays the same for long periods of time. As our models learned and improved, they uncovered lots of suspicious recording gaps. In the end, we documented more than 250 camera obstructions. Moments like these are exactly the situations that body cameras are meant to document, helping ensure that any unlawful behavior is captured and that circumstances surrounding the 122 killings can be properly investigated. Another method we used was an AI system that analyzes audio to detect gunshots. After we trained it specifically for Rio police body cameras and local conditions, the model successfully detected most gunshots in a test set of videos. We were also able to use AI to pull text directly from the videos, like the date, time, location and ID number of the officer wearing the camera. But one of the most striking findings came from what we didn't see. Despite the scale of the operation and the number of deaths, we found no footage showing the killings themselves. NARRATION To understand what was missing, we organized body camera recordings across the operation using extracted timestamps. TEXT ON SCREEN Unusable footage Usable footage NARRATION We found that more than half the officers’ recordings had either ended or had significant gaps by noon. From there, the usable footage continued to decline, just as the operation became most deadly. The missing footage, combined with extensive evidence of camera tampering, suggests that body cameras were deliberately misused to prevent killings from being recorded. Throughout our investigation, AI was one tool out of many. Our team of researchers interviewed witnesses in Rio, visited the neighborhood where the killings took place, analyzed police records and autopsies, verified photographs and videos, and manually reviewed AI findings. What AI provided was speed and scale. It helped us process thousands of hours of footage, connect pieces of evidence, and focus our attention where it mattered most. In other words, AI helped us find needles in a very large haystack. Now, it's up to Brazilian prosecutors to thoroughly investigate both the killings and the decisions that led to such a deadly operation. Those who use disproportionate force or misuse body cameras should be held accountable. To learn more about the events of October 28th and Human Rights Watch’s findings, visit HRW.org and read our investigation, A Strategy of Death. Police officers tampered with body cameras and were responsible for serious investigative failures during an operation ostensibly to arrest gang members in a low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro on October 28, 2025. A year-long Human Rights Watch investigation concluded that police breached Supreme Court orders and their own protocols during Operation Containment, which appeared to be lethal by design. Federal and state prosecutors should initiate criminal and civil proceedings to investigate those responsible for abuses, including senior officials and police commanders. (Rio de Janeiro, October 28, 2026) – Police officers tampered with body cameras and failed to take crucial investigative steps during an operation in a low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on October 28, 2025, Human Rights Watch said in an investigation published today. Evidence indicates police used excessive force and may have intentionally killed scores of men and boys. The investigation, “‘A Strategy of Death’: Investigating Brazil’s Deadliest Police Operation,” documents Operation Containment (Operação Contenção), in which a total of 122 people were killed. This included two children and four police officers killed that day, and a fifth police officer who later succumbed to his wounds. An additional two men were killed in the early morning before the official start of the operation. Eighty-five percent of non-police victims of the October 2025 raid were Black. “A Strategy of Death” Investigating Brazil’s Deadliest Police Operation Read the full investigation here None of the killings were captured in the thousands of hours of body camera footage sent by Rio de Janeiro Military Police to the Public Defender’s Office, which Human Rights Watch reviewed after being granted access. “Human Rights Watch processed thousands of hours of body camera footage and analyzed videos, official investigation files, and autopsy records for every victim, yet crucial questions remain because police failed to properly record killings, preserve crime scenes, or collect crucial data,” said Sophia Jones, open source researcher with the Digital Investigations Lab at Human Rights Watch. “The families of those killed, including police officers, deserve answers and accountability with a thorough, independent investigation.” Human Rights Watch interviewed 41 witnesses, family members, and experts, and analyzed 4,400 hours of body camera footage, 9,000 pages of official investigation files, 122 autopsy reports, court records, and hundreds of videos and photographs. Human Rights Watch analyzed the data using several machine learning models built in-house, followed by manual review and assessment by researchers. Based on Human Rights Watch analysis of data from Rio-based security research lab GENI (Grupo de Estudos dos Novos Ilegalismos or Group for the Study of New Illegalities), nongovernmental think tank Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública (Brazilian Public Security Forum), independent security monitoring organization Fogo Cruzado (Crossfire), and media reports, Operation Containment was the deadliest documented one-day police operation in a country where police forces kill more than 6,000 people per year. Human Rights Watch visited the Complexo da Penha, the site of the operation, six months after the raid and found that the criminal group Red Command (Comando Vermelho)—the target of the operation—continued to impose its rule on residents. Despite the stated goal of carrying out 100 arrest warrants for alleged Red Command members, police records show they arrested only 17 of those for whom they had warrants, although it is not clear whether those are the warrants that justified the operation or other pending warrants. Police did not enter the home of the local Red Command leader, for whom they had a warrant, a Civil Police commander told prosecutors, even though body camera footage shows police moving around it. Despite a state law and a Supreme Court order mandating that police wear body cameras, only about 23 percent of the 2,500 civil and military police officers who participated in the raid did, the Rio de Janeiro government said. Machine-Enabled Forensics How Human Rights Watch used Artificial Intelligence to Analyze Body Camera Footage from Rio’s Deadliest Police Raid Read the methodology here Human Rights Watch analysis of the footage of the 527 military police officers who wore the cameras found widespread tampering and obstruction of their use. Officers left cameras running before the operation, effectively draining batteries; covered lenses; placed cameras where they would not capture officers’ actions; and left cameras in vehicles. Such tampering consistently occurred at key moments, during arrests, shootouts, or while officers entered homes, researchers found. Most tampering was on cameras worn by officers whose units engaged in frontline operations, such as the Battalion of Special Police Operations of the Military Police, the unit deployed to the forested area where the majority of killings took place. Researchers determined that 36 percent of gunshot clusters heard on their cameras occurred when the cameras were obstructed. Body camera footage showed officers assaulting and threatening to kill detainees, including a child, whom they forced to lie down next to a dead body while photographing him. In another recording, an officer tells officers to shoot detainees in the legs if they ran. In a third clip, an officer expressed frustration that body cameras prevented them from killing suspects. Researchers also analyzed or verified hundreds of videos and photographs taken by members of the local community that day. In one series of verified videos, officers pile dead bodies, some with their genitalia exposed, into an armored police vehicle, while joking. “Look how wonderful,” one officer said. “We like this.” While police said they spent months planning the operation, there was no evidence that they made any advance preparations to protect crime scenes and conduct forensic analysis. In addition, Civil Police failed to collect basic information for all but two of the 117 non-police victims, such as the names of police officers and residents who brought some of them to a hospital. Only seven suspects were taken to a hospital and subsequently arrested, compared with 117 people killed by police. That unusually high ratio of people killed to people injured (17 to 1) raises serious questions about whether police prioritized lethal force over arresting suspects. An analysis of victim autopsy reports also points in that direction. Over 40 percent of non-police victims in the reports analyzed were shot in the head, over 60 percent were shot four or more times, and nearly 75 percent were shot at least once on the back. One man was shot and then decapitated. According to forensic experts from the Independent Forensic Expert Group of the International Rehabilitation Council for Torture Victims consulted by Human Rights Watch, the evidence suggests that many were targeted and killed intentionally. In many instances, the trajectory of gunshot wounds was from bottom to top, which can be indicative of execution, such as when an individual is shot while lying down or otherwise incapacitated. Brazilian authorities should ensure a thorough and independent investigation into the planning and decisions by senior officials and police commanders that led to the deadly operation. Rio de Janeiro’s new governor, who will take office on January 6, 2027, should introduce a bill to separate forensic services from the Civil Police. “Our investigation shows police flouted the law and their own protocols during the disastrous raid,” said César Muñoz, Brazil director at Human Rights Watch. “Abusive police practices undermine public security by making communities less willing to collaborate with police, while fueling a cycle of violence that endangers both residents and police officers. Brazil needs new effective public security strategies that uphold human rights.”

Alarming Attacks on Women Politicians. Click to expand Image Ana Elisa Santos Silva of the Workers' Party (PT), the youngest federal deputy elected in Minas Gerais state, poses for a photograph in Divinopolis, Brazil, on October 15, 2026. © 2026 Douglas Magno/AFP via Getty Images Overwhelmed by threats—and fearing for her personal safety Satya Rhodes-Conway the current mayor of Madison, Wisconsin in the US, announced on October 23 that she was dropping her bid for reelection. "The price of being in public office has gotten too high,” she said. Globally, women in public life face alarming levels of political violence, including tech-facilitated sexual and gender-based violence, with little protection or recourse. While research finds chillingly high rates of violence against both women and men in politics, women are at greater risk and face more sexualized and gendered violence. After Australian MP Helen Haines was deliberately hit by a car, doctors had to amputate both of her legs. In South Africa, a bloody campaign season included the killing of party activist Jeanette Magugu and a brutal home invasion against mayoral candidate Nhongo Solo. In Brazil, Ana Elisa Santos Silva and other candidates for public office filed police complaints about death and sexual violence threats on the campaign trail; a city councilor, Iara Pimentel, closed her X account due to threats and was hospitalized after a brick hit her at a rally. Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a US congressional candidate in Arizona, reported that she was attacked while repairing campaign posters and raped. While attackers’ motives are often unclear, the result is the same--women and girls who speak up for their communities increasingly experience gendered violence and threats. After a 15-year-old made a video crudely lambasting India’s Prime Minister, she was inundated with rape and death threats. An Iraqi women’s rights leader who challenged an abusive amendment to Iraq’s personal status law was shot dead outside her home. Technological developments also fuel gendered abuses. Of 720 European Parliament members, 46 women and four men had been depicted in or seen their online presence linked to deep fake sexualized images, according to a 2026 study. In the Asia-Pacific region, 18 percent of participating women parliamentarians faced doxing, according to a study. These crimes are taking place amid a global backlash against women’s rights, with political power for women declining in many countries. After years of progress, the percentage of women national cabinet members globally declined to 22 percent in 2026, from 23 percent in 2024. Experts increasingly warn that political violence deters women from running for office. With growing evidence that women’s leadership brings economic and social benefits, we all lose when women are pushed out of politics.

UAE: UN Secretary-General Candidate Whitewashed Abuses. Click to expand Image Lana Zaki Nusseibeh, representative to the United Nations of the United Arab Emirates, speaks during a UN Security Council meeting at UN headquarters on February 23, 2023. © 2023 John Minchillo/AP Photo (Beirut) – Lana Zaki Nusseibeh, a long-serving UAE diplomat and foreign affairs official, has an extensive record of denying and whitewashing the country’s rights abuses in Sudan and Yemen, Human Rights Watch said today. On October 21, 2026, the UAE formally nominated Nusseibeh to be the new United Nations secretary-general. “For years, Lana Nusseibeh has used her position to vehemently deny and divert attention from the UAE’s war crimes in Yemen and support for the abusive Rapid Support Forces in Sudan,” said Bruno Stagno Ugarte, chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch. “Her disinformation about the UAE’s rights record, particularly her dismissal of the UN’s own reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF, has seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims.” Nusseibeh has repeatedly denied that the UAE provides military support to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, while refusing to address clear evidence to the contrary. The RSF, engaged in a conflict with the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF), is responsible for widespread war crimes and crimes against humanity, including as part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing in the Darfur region. The United Nations Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan concluded that their assault on the North Darfur capital of El Fasher “bore the hallmarks of genocide.” In September 2024, Nusseibeh said in a letter to the editor of The Economist that, “[T]he UAE is not providing weapons or any other support to the Rapid Support Forces or any of the warring parties in Sudan.” The letter followed the publication of the first UN Panel of Experts on Sudan’s report, which included conclusions of “credible allegations” that the UAE was providing military support to the RSF through Chad. A UAE government letter from December 2023 in the report annex claims that flights from the UAE to Chad transported humanitarian assistance to Sudanese civilians. The letter is unsigned but bears the letterhead of the Permanent Mission of the UAE to the UN in New York. Nusseibeh was the head of the UAE’s mission from 2013 until April 2024. In April 2024, in response to accusations from the government of Sudan that the UAE was providing the RSF with military, logistical, and political support, Nusseibeh said in a statement that the “claims were baseless” and affirmed the UAE’s categorical rejection “of the false allegations.” In July 2024, asked by CNN whether the UAE was arming the RSF, Nusseibeh replied: “No, those allegations are categorically untrue. The UAE, as it has done in countless places around the world when there is a humanitarian crisis, has projected humanitarian aid in as quickly as possible and then scaled that way.” In November 2025, as a minister of state, Nusseibeh took part in an Emirati “lobbying blitz” with key European Parliament members that said that the UAE was “playing a constructive role in Sudan” in the lead up to a vote on a resolution condemning atrocities in Sudan, according to Politico. The European Parliament passed the resolution without mention of the UAE’s role in the conflict.
